versions.body:
# Notification Display and Template Rendering Decision

During the stabilization window, application notification display and Issue Template Hash Rendering came up at the same time. Do not treat the two as the same change yet. Notification text on the page deals with settings the application has already saved; the template deals with rendering input supplied by the caller. They may appear on the same page, but the objects and gaps are different.

Three arrangements were compared initially.

- The wrapped App retains the notification configuration; the decorator only turns the existing value into page text; the template gets the hash from the caller.
- Have the decorator also guess the notification rules and template fields, and return a unified display object.
- Have the template look up the App and the complete issue object itself, no longer requiring the caller to specify the input.

Tentatively choose the first. The second eliminates one entry point but conflates configuration facts, page text, and template input into the same context. The third looks convenient, but once the template is accustomed to finding the complete object itself, passing a hash from the caller is merely a coding convenience; it cannot express the boundary "only this content is delivered here."

"Display" does not mean that the notification has been sent. If the page can read the threshold, that only shows it retrieved the configuration and performed some kind of formatting; whether email or another delivery occurred must be determined from the respective path. Successful delivery likewise cannot prove that the page used the correct display content.

An old troubleshooting note left `lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` as a checkpoint for authentication failures. Keep this entry point, but just because the filename and failure symptom are adjacent, we cannot attribute the authentication-failure coverage file to issue template rendering, nor conclude from that that it is responsible for notification display.

When fields are missing from the hash, do not casually fill in a set of business defaults in the template. An absent notification threshold may be a valid configuration; if the template did not receive the agreed fields, the caller's handoff may be incomplete. Both can look empty on the page, but they are handled in different places.

The parameter name `user` in the issue tracker creation API should not be inferred to be a generic key for the template hash. Both sides involve issue objects; that does not mean their input shapes are the same.

It still needs to be confirmed whether the object obtained by the authentication-failure page changes when the decorator is called; there is not enough recorded evidence yet.

# Decision on Notification Display and Template Rendering

The initial brief note grouped the application decorator and issue templates together because both were raised during the stabilization window. After review, the earlier separation still holds: application configuration, page display, and template input are not the same object. However, the first version only said they should not be merged; it did not record why a single "convenient helper" could not address every gap, nor did it explain where the authentication failure override path belonged.

## The Earlier Trade-offs Still Hold

The facts about notification thresholds should remain in App. The page needs a readable result, so the decorator can organize known configuration into display content; it should not redefine notification rules on App's behalf. Templates handle their own input. If the caller supplies only the fields a template needs, the template does not need to look back to the complete issue object just to appear general-purpose.

We considered letting templates read App directly. This would make notification settings available on every render, seemingly reducing the caller's work in preparing a hash. But the template would then depend on the issue object, application configuration, and calling environment at the same time; when another entry point did not have a complete App, it would be difficult to tell which item was missing. This approach was not adopted.

We also considered having the decorator return a unified "notification context". It would contain notification thresholds, commonly used template fields, and the display text needed by the authentication failure page. At the time, this proposal seemed to reduce duplication, but it collapsed empty values from different sources into the same result. An empty string might mean the application truly had no configuration, that the template had not received a field, or simply that the authentication failure path had not created the page object. Once the page saw only the unified result, it would lose the starting point for tracing the cause.

There was another variation at the time: instead of returning text directly, the unified helper would return a large hash, and the page and template would each take the parts they needed. This variation still did not change the problem. The helper would first need to know which fields came from App, which came from the issue object, and which existed only on authentication failure; in trying to fill the large hash, it could easily replace content that the caller should explicitly supply with implicit lookups. Changing the output format from a string to a hash would not make the sources clear again.

## A Hash Is Not an Alias for the Complete Object

The purpose of letting an issue template accept a hash is not to give the complete object a shorter notation, but to let the caller explicitly supply a limited set of inputs. The template can consume this content, but should not treat an object that was not supplied as an inherently available fallback source.

This does not require every template to use the same set of keys. Different templates may care about only part of an issue; listing every possible field in a permanent table would instead make it easy to mistake unused fields for required ones. Field selection should follow the specific template and its call site, rather than expand along with the page display layer.

The limited scope of the hash has another practical benefit: when reading a template, readers can first see the dependencies it acknowledges, rather than work backward from the page, authentication logic, and issue object to guess them. If the caller has prepared too few fields, the first step should be to supply the missing ones at the call site or adjust the template's expectations; the template itself should not cross the input boundary on the grounds that "there is a complete object nearby anyway". This leaves more work at the call sites, but also prevents a template from silently using different data sources at different entry points.

Missing keys must not be confused with empty configuration. When a template has not received the content its contract requires, first check why the caller did not supply it; only when the application has configuration but the decorator cannot produce a readable result should the decorator's formatting be checked. The former means the input was not properly supplied; the latter means an existing object was not displayed correctly.

An empty array must also be distinguished from the absence of a value. An application having no notification thresholds can be a valid state, and must not be treated as an error merely because the page has no text to display. Conversely, if a field required by the template is absent, that must not be hidden behind the same empty text. The two states may end up looking similar, but the direction of investigation should not be the same.

## The Retained Old Proposal

> Give notification thresholds, the template hash, and the copy needed by the authentication failure page to the same helper; the helper retrieves values, fills in defaults, and outputs a string, while the page and template no longer concern themselves with the sources.

This proposal no longer applies, but is retained here. Its mistake was not outputting a string, but deciding on the same defaulting strategy for three objects in advance. An application with no notification configuration, a caller that selected the wrong subset of fields, and an authentication override page that did not obtain the expected object may require different handling; the unified helper would first turn all of them into indistinguishable display results.

The old proposal also reversed the reading direction. Originally, readers could first ask, "Is this App's configuration, the template's input, or the authentication failure page's object?"; with the helper, they could only trace backward from empty text to every possible source. The early preference for it arose because neither the page nor the template had a clear entry point, and merging them seemed easier than identifying each layer separately. That motivation is understandable, but it cannot continue to serve as the basis for the boundaries.

The fact that two call sites both need to display text does not mean they should share defaults. Page text comes from the form of App's configuration; template text comes from the hash prepared by the caller. Even if both ultimately display the same words, that is not enough to merge responsibility for preparing the data.

## Authentication Failure Override Checkpoint

`lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` remains as an earlier entry point for investigation. It is related to authentication failure, so it may affect when the page reaches the decorator; the existing material has not established that it has direct responsibility for issue template rendering. Previously, placing the path and the template in the same paragraph could create the impression that "the file is right next to it, so it should be responsible". Now, only its adjacency is retained.

This is also why decisions should not be inferred from path names. The authentication failure override, App decorator, and issue template may be read during the same request, but similar names and adjacent pages are not enough to prove that they share implementation responsibilities. If display differences arise on the authentication failure page in the future, the object the page actually receives and its view entry point should be recorded separately.

What needs to be checked in the authentication failure path is whether it changes when the page object is created or when the page reaches the decorator; it does not need to interpret issue fields for the template, nor should it become the source of truth for App configuration. Keeping this checkpoint in the decision record is intended to avoid overlooking an adjacent entry point during investigation, not to expand the file's responsibilities.

## Decisions for This Round

1. App remains the source of truth for notification configuration; the decorator is responsible for passing the displayable parts to the page.
2. Issue templates may accept hashes selected by callers; templates must not use defaults to hide content the caller did not supply.
3. The authentication failure override file serves only as an adjacent checkpoint and is outside the scope of responsibility for template rendering.
4. Configuration text displayed on a page must not be interpreted as confirmation that email, hook, or other delivery has completed.

This decision does not specify the fields for every template, nor does it define final copy for every empty array. The former belongs to each template's local input; the latter first requires checking whether an empty array represents valid configuration on the page. Prematurely turning these two unresolved questions into a unified rule would only repeat the old proposal's mistake.

The `user` parameter on the issue tracker creation side remains within its own interface boundary. Do not add it to every template hash just because its name seems suited to an issue object; a template's fields should be determined by the content the template needs.

# Notification Display and Template Rendering Decision

This record has not been consolidated into a single page specification. It spans several stabilization windows, preserving how a set of adjacent objects was understood at different times: how pages read an application's notification configuration, why issue templates accept hashes, and why the authentication failure override file was once mistakenly placed at the center of the discussion. Some judgments in the older text are no longer valid, but remain in their original positions; deleting them would leave later readers with only the conclusions, without showing how the boundaries became confused.

The initial confusion came from the word "notification." Some used it to mean the thresholds saved in the App, some meant the text displayed on the page, and others meant messages that had already been sent. All three objects can appear on the same page, so the fact that a page could display the configuration was easily written up as evidence that delivery was working; a template displaying a particular field was also easily written up as evidence that the template should have the complete issue object. The focus of the subsequent additions was not to introduce a larger context, but to separate these seemingly continuous things again.

This decision addresses only two handoff boundaries: the handoff from the wrapped App to the presentation layer, and the handoff from the caller to the issue template. The authentication failure override path is retained as an adjacent checkpoint. Email, hooks, issue tracker creation, and page objects outside templates are not automatically included in the same decision simply because their names are similar.

## The Earliest Trade-offs

The initial record proposed three options.

- The wrapped App stores the notification configuration, and the decorator only organizes content for display; the template receives a hash from the caller.
- The decorator infers both notification rules and template fields, returning a unified display context.
- The template looks up the App and the complete issue object itself, no longer requiring the caller to specify the input.

The first option was provisionally selected at the time. It did not claim that the decorator was the source of all page data, only that the decorator sits at the presentation boundary and is suited to passing the existing configuration structure to the view. The template does not need to know the complete object; since the caller chooses to pass a hash, it can make explicit what is actually being supplied here.

The second option was attractive at the time. Both pages and templates needed to display text, and the authentication failure page appeared in nearby troubleshooting notes. Having one helper centralize value retrieval, fill in defaults, and produce text seemed easier than confirming sources layer by layer. It was not adopted immediately, not because of opposition to shared code, but because there was no answer to what the helper should actually represent when faced with a null value.

The third option was also set aside. Having the template read the complete App or issue object itself would reduce the caller's work in preparing a hash, but would make the template depend on its calling environment. When one entry point has a complete object and another supplies only partial content, the template's behavior would differ silently; readers of the template would have difficulty knowing what it actually depends on.

The earliest version left only one unresolved question: whether an empty array and a missing field are equivalent. Both may result in no text on the page, but they come from different sources. An application having no notification thresholds may be a valid configuration; a template not receiving a value it is contractually expected to receive may mean that the caller's input is incomplete. There was not enough reason to collapse these two states into a single default text.

A side note from the same period added `lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` to the record. Earlier troubleshooting would lead from authentication failure symptoms to this file, so it was a checkpoint worth retaining. At the time, it had not been confirmed whether it passed through the App decorator, nor whether it participated in issue template rendering. The path was recorded so that the timing of page object creation could be revisited when reviewing authentication failures later, not to assign implementation ownership for notification display or template rendering.

## First Side Note: Page Display Is Not a Delivery Receipt

In an early discussion, there was an overly broad claim: "If the page can display the notification settings, that means the notification pipeline is working." This statement was later narrowed, but part of its original intent remains useful: if the page can display the content, that at least indicates that the presentation layer obtained some configuration it can represent.

It can no longer carry any further meaning. The notification text on the page does not prove that an email was delivered, does not prove that a hook request completed, and does not prove that other output paths use the same formatting. They may read from the same App data, or they may each fail in different places. Sharing a configuration source does not mean sharing the same result.

The reverse inference is also invalid. Even if a particular delivery succeeds, that cannot confirm the separation of notification thresholds, the visible entry point, or the display style on the page. The delivery path is concerned with sending, while the page path is concerned with a readable result; treating one as validation of the other will cause page issues to be masked when delivery succeeds, and will cause delivery issues to be mistakenly considered resolved when the page works normally.

This note does not require the page to stop displaying notification settings. It only specifies that the page display should be read as the presentation layer's own result. If the page text is wrong, first check the App's existing configuration and the decorator's assembly; if the message was not sent, follow the corresponding delivery path. The same conclusion that "notifications are working" cannot be used to close both checks.

## Split After Review

The subsequent review kept the original direction and clarified two boundaries. First, the App is the source of truth for notification configuration. A decorator can organize existing values into content suitable for reading on the page, but it cannot decide new notification rules on the App's behalf during presentation. Second, a template hash is a local interface between the caller and the template, not an abbreviation of the complete issue object.

Organizing the hash by template means calling Fang Ke to deliver only the content required for that rendering. This does not require all templates to have the same set of keys. Different templates may care only about local information from the issue; merging every field that has ever appeared into a permanent large table would instead cause fields not used by a particular template to be mistaken for required dependencies.

This choice has a cost. The caller needs to be clear about what it has prepared, and the template cannot treat objects that were not provided as an ad hoc fallback source. The review accepted this cost because narrowing the input occurs at the call site, where it can be located and discussed; if the template secretly looks back up the complete object, the same template will receive different implicit inputs depending on the entry point.

Here, "hash" does not mean that a template can receive only a small amount of information, nor does it mean that the input must always be trimmed to the same degree. It means that the input boundary is determined jointly by that template and its corresponding call site. When the fields a template needs change, the change should first be made explicit at that template's call site, rather than having the template fill in the gaps on its own from application settings, the authentication path, or the complete issue object.

During the review, someone suggested having the decorator return a large hash, with the page and templates each retrieving their own values, to avoid the unified helper outputting only text. This variant was not adopted. Changing text to a hash does not restore provenance: the helper would still need to determine in advance which fields come from the App, which come from the issue object, and which exist only on the authentication-failure path. To make the large hash "complete," it would still encourage implicit lookups and unified default values.

## Deprecated: Unified Helper

The original text of the proposal from that time is retained below. It is no longer applicable.

> To reduce duplication, provide the notification thresholds, issue-template inputs, and display content required by the authentication-failure page through a single helper. The helper is responsible for retrieving values, filling in defaults, and generating text; the page and templates no longer distinguish where the data comes from.

This approach was later rejected, not because there was anything wrong with the output string itself, but because it first chose the same default strategy for three different objects. An App with no notification configuration, a caller that omitted a template field, and an authentication failure page that did not obtain the expected object would all first become the same blank text. When readers saw an empty result, they could not tell whether they should go back to the configuration, the caller, or the authentication path.

The old approach also reversed the reading direction. Originally, one could first ask, "Is this the App's configuration, the template's input, or an object created by the authentication failure page?"; after using the helper, one could only work backward from a piece of blank text toward every possible source. The reason it was favored early on was that the page and template lacked clear entry points, so merging them seemed easier than distinguishing them layer by layer. That motivation is understandable, but it cannot continue to serve as the basis for the boundary.

Another problem with the unified helper is that it disguises different fixes as the same kind of work. If the configuration exists but the decorator cannot express it, formatting may need to be checked; if the template lacks a required field, the caller may need to be reviewed; if the authentication failure page did not create the expected object, the path itself needs to be checked. All three can cause readers to see a blank, but they cannot be replaced by the same default value in one place.

This old approach is retained here without providing a new generic replacement. If shared helper logic really needs to be extracted in the future, first state whether it serves App configuration interpretation, page formatting by the decorator, or template input construction. Do not once again assume that "all displayed content is one kind of context."

## A counterexample left by one actual review

During the review, the notification text on the page was once treated as a signal that "the notification had no problem." That judgment was too broad. At most, the page shows that there is no obvious discrepancy in the presentation layer; it cannot show that message delivery occurred. Nor can the delivery result confirm the separators, styling, or visible entry point on the page. When two paths use the same application configuration, they are especially easy to misread as a single conclusion.

There is a similar counterexample on the template side. If the template receives a hash but, when a key is missing, bypasses the hash to look up the complete issue object, a single page may still continue to render. Only when another call site intentionally passes just the truncated content does the template expose that it depended on an object that was never delivered. The problem is not that "the hash is not complete enough," but that the template crossed the input boundary defined by the caller.

The review therefore withdrew another blanket statement: not every case of a missing value should be handled by the caller. A value for which the configuration exists but the decorator cannot express it belongs to the form that the presentation layer needs to handle; when the template has not received a key that it specifies as required, the caller should be reviewed first. Both results may display as empty, but the point where they should be diagnosed is different.

This does not mean that every empty array should be treated as an anomaly. The application may genuinely have no notification threshold; that state cannot be rewritten as a caller error merely because the page has no text. Conversely, the fact that the page must accommodate a valid empty configuration does not mean that a missing template key should be silently swallowed. A valid empty configuration and an undelivered input must retain different directions for follow-up.

The authentication-failure override file also came up again during the review. It can continue to serve as a checkpoint for the old path, used to confirm whether authentication failure changed when the page reached the decorator; it cannot become the rendering owner of the issue template merely because the paths are adjacent, much less take on responsibility for formatting the notification threshold. This corrects the original file annotation; it does not rename the file's purpose.

## Meeting margin notes, not organized into a specification

The meeting did not leave a line-by-line record, only the following brief statements that were repeatedly confirmed:

- Displayed configuration is not a delivery receipt.
- A hash is not an alias for the complete object.
- For now, treat the authentication-failure override file only as a checkpoint.

The first sentence does not mean that the page does not need to display notification settings. The page should still present readable configuration to the user; it just should not turn readability into a delivery guarantee. The second sentence also does not require the template to reject partial input; partial input is an allowed choice and only requires the caller and template to share an understanding of the necessary content. The third sentence prevents the similarity between filenames and observed behavior from being mistakenly written as a call relationship.

After the meeting, someone suggested maintaining a permanent field table for all problem-related fields. That suggestion was not incorporated into the decision. The problem template's hash is a local interface, and different templates may not share the same fields; a single large table would turn fields that happen to appear into long-term prerequisites. When a field list is genuinely needed, it should be maintained alongside the specific template and its call sites, rather than being predefined by the page presentation layer.

Someone else proposed first converting the authentication failure page into a "standard page context" and then passing it to the decorator and template. That proposal has the same difficulty as the unified helper: the so-called standard context would first have to decide, on behalf of different entry points, what counts as missing, what counts as a default, and what counts as a retrievable object. It does not solve the object boundary; it merely moves the boundary to a harder-to-locate place, so it was not pursued further.

## Corrected Default-Value Assessment

Early on, there was an informal practice: when a template encountered an empty value, it supplied a safe empty string, and when a page encountered an empty list, it displayed the same text. The motivation was to prevent a single missing field from immediately breaking the display, but this is no longer appropriate.

The problem is that it collapses "no displayable content" and "content that should have been received" into the same visual result. A valid empty configuration is mistaken for a caller error, while a caller's failure to pass a field is mistaken for a normal empty state. Conversely, treating every empty list as an error is also wrong, because the application may genuinely have no notification thresholds.

After the correction, no additional universal fallback is added. The App preserves the actual configuration state; given the existing configuration shape, the decorator organizes the displayable parts for the page; and the template consumes the hash explicitly delivered by the caller. If the template is missing a key, check the caller first; if a configuration value cannot be represented, check the decorator first. Fixes in the two directions do not have to produce the same page text.

This is also why the application decorator and the problem template can be documented in the same decision, but should not share a single implementation commitment. Their boundaries meet, and the page may use both the decorator's result and the template's output at the same time; but one handles the handoff from the wrapped App to the presentation layer, while the other handles the handoff from the caller to the template.

Defaults are not categorically prohibited. The current record only rejects using the same default to flatten missing values from different sources. If a template explicitly designs a field as optional, that should be expressed in the template and its call sites; if an App configuration allows an empty value, the presentation layer should handle it according to its configuration shape. This decision must not turn these local choices into a uniform strategy across objects.

## Legacy Examples Still Retained

### Legacy example: The template assembles the notification list itself

Early on, it was suggested that the notification array be passed directly to the template, with the template assembling it and handling empty values. This example is obsolete. It makes the template decide the separators, formatting, and empty state; if the page also needs to display the same information, there will be two similar but not necessarily consistent formatting implementations. Whether the notification list should be passed to the template must be explicitly decided by the caller; page display should not be copied into the template by default.

What is misleading about this legacy example is not that the template can never display notification-related content, but that it treats page display responsibilities as the template's natural input. If the template genuinely needs notification information, the caller should explicitly place it in that invocation's hash; the template cannot retrieve the App's full configuration on its own just because a decorator already exists nearby on the page.

### Legacy example: The complete problem object is always next to the template

Another old note assumed that the full issue object was always available when rendering an issue template, so the hash was merely a convenience in notation. That assumption no longer applies. A hash can be an intentionally reduced input, and the template must not treat an object that the caller did not supply as a fallback source.

This old example is retained to explain why "a single page can still render" does not prove that input boundaries are irrelevant. The fact that one entry point happens to have the full object only shows that its environment is richer; it does not legitimize the template's implicit dependencies at other entry points.

### Old example: the authentication failure file is the central entry point for display logic

This example comes from early file navigation, not a verified implementation relationship. It remains here because investigators may still reach this file through an authentication failure symptom. The correct way to read it is to first check the request path and view object, then determine whether a decorator is involved; notification display or template rendering must not be attributed to that file based solely on its location.

The existence of `lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` still has practical value: when the authentication failure page shows display differences, it can be used to check when the page object is created. It does not provide a source for template fields, nor does it automatically include the authentication failure page in the display pipeline for ordinary pages. An old entry point can help locate the issue, but that does not mean it defines the responsibilities of all adjacent objects.

## Decision for the current stabilization window

The records retained above have already distinguished configuration facts from delivery results, page text from structured template inputs, and authentication failure checkpoints from rendering ownership. Within the stabilization window, the decision is limited to the decorator's display responsibilities; it does not expand the scope to include template fields, delivery actions, or authentication override paths.

AppDecorator must expose email_at_notices from the wrapped App, format the notification threshold array as `1, 3`, and maintain the visibility styles of notify_user_display and notify_err_display.

This decision requires existing pages to retain access to these two display entry points, and requires the threshold array to be displayed using the existing comma-and-space format. It does not require issue templates to convert notification thresholds into the same text, does not interpret page visibility as proof that a message has been delivered, and does not authorize the decorator to rewrite the App's notification rules.

The state sequence in the diagram only represents how the page display reads existing configuration. It does not indicate that email or other notification paths have completed, nor does it indicate that the authentication failure override file must pass through this sequence.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> app_config
    app_config: App configuration
    app_config --> decorator_display
    decorator_display: Decorator display
    decorator_display --> page_view
    page_view: Page
    page_view --> [*]
```

Formatting notification arrays falls under the decorator display responsibility because the page needs stable, readable results, not because the arrays themselves are part of the template protocol. If a template wants to display the same type of information, the caller should still decide whether to provide it and which fields to provide; the template cannot treat an existing page display entry as its implicit data source.

Visibility styling is also a local page responsibility. It maintains how notification settings are displayed on the page; it does not provide a success marker for message delivery, promise the authentication-failure path that the same object has been established, or fill in fields for the issue template. Separating these three types of concerns is precisely why this consolidation retains the old records.

## The Narrow Decision on Template Inputs

The issue template keeps its decision narrow: call Fang Ke to provide the fields the template actually needs. The template should not look up the complete issue object or infer App configuration simply because a field was not provided. When adding a new template, first specify where the hash is constructed and which fields the caller guarantees, and then decide whether to reuse the existing construction logic.

No unified issue hash is established here, nor are field names defined for all templates. The appearance of a field in one template is not enough to make it a prerequisite for another template. When a template needs richer input, the corresponding call site should be expanded to provide it, rather than bypassing the input boundary through a lookup inside the template.

The `user` parameter in the issue tracker creation interface belongs to the tracker integration boundary. Having the same field name does not make it a universal key for all issue templates, nor can it be used to supply a default value for template input. The meaning of the creation interface's parameters is determined by the tracker integration; the meaning of the template hash's fields is determined by the template and the caller. The two cannot be merged simply because both concern the issue object.

The decision about the template hash likewise does not prescribe the page's wording. When the page displays the notification threshold, the decorator handles the shape of the App configuration; when the template renders issue content, the template handles the input provided by the caller. They may appear together on the same page, but that does not mean they can share one complete object, one null-value strategy, or one set of fields.

## Adjacent Items Not Included in This Decision

It is still unconfirmed whether the page necessarily receives the same decorator context as a normal request when authentication failure goes through the override path.`lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` remains a checkpoint; if differences appear in the authentication failure page's presentation, record the objects and view entry points for that path separately, then determine whether they fall within the scope of this decision.

The permanent set of fields for the template hash is not defined here either. Different issue templates may require different local content, and consolidating guesses into a shared field table would once again blur the caller's responsibility. Page notification presentation, email delivery, hook request bodies, and issue tracker creation each retain their own output boundaries, even when they share an issue object.

There is another unresolved point: if the authentication failure path does affect when the decorator is reached, first confirm whether it changes the page object, the view entry point, or the location of the decorator call, then discuss whether the presentation needs to be adjusted. The occurrence of an authentication failure does not directly imply that template inputs should also change, much less justify restoring the old unified helper approach.

This record retains old examples and approaches, but that does not mean they can still serve as default implementations. They only explain why configuration, presentation, templates, and authentication paths were combined in one place in the past. The scope of the current decision ends here: App configuration becomes page presentation through decorators; issue templates are rendered using the hash supplied by the caller; authentication failure override files remain adjacent entry points that need to be checked separately.

# API key rotation review proposal

For this round, start by discussing API key rotation and Application watcher Relationship Query in the same trial plan. Both begin with the application object, but one changes persistent state while the other merely reads a relationship; they should not share a return contract just because the entry points are close.

On the rotation side, there are two candidate directions: have the application generate and save the new key itself, or have the caller generate it and hand it back for saving. The former makes it easier to put the old value, new value, and save result in one operation; the latter spreads the key-generation rules across callers. We lean toward the former, but we do not yet have a complete sample of existing calls.

Restrict the watcher query to an entry point that reads application relationships. We need to confirm whether an empty relationship returns an empty collection, an empty value, or is handled separately by the caller; this will affect page display and subsequent API examples. Do not treat "no watcher" as an incidental signal of rotation failure.

Spell out the rollback conditions as well: if the new key cannot be read back after saving, or if the query entry forces the caller to depend on transient state during rotation, stop merging the trial and revert to two separate changes. An old troubleshooting pass once pointed to `lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb`; record it provisionally as a verification entry point, not as a basis for deciding implementation ownership.

# API Key Rotation Review Plan

After review, the previous version overstated that "the application object is the common entry point." A common entry point only means that the two operations touch the same object; it does not mean they should share an interface, transaction, or error handling. The plan now has two parallel trial tracks: one handles only key replacement and storage; the other only determines who consumes the watcher relationship query.

The rotation track retains three checkpoints: the old key can be obtained before the call; the generated value differs from the old value; and reading again after the save completes still returns the new value. The return value needs to be explicit. The caller should not have to infer whether the operation succeeded from whether the key is empty. If generation, writing, and returning the value are split across layers, it is difficult to tell after a failure whether to retain the old key or generate a new one.

We previously considered passing the new key to the UI layer first and having the UI trigger the save. This would make temporary display convenient, but it would allow an unsaved value to enter more call paths and make it harder to determine whether a retry produced a second key. The trial prioritizes keeping generation and persistence on the application side; the UI or integration side only receives the result after the operation. This choice has not been extended to other authentication behavior.

The watcher query is not part of the rotation success criteria. The query interface needs to provide a stable relationship shape so that the caller Fang Ke can distinguish between "the application has no watcher" and "the query itself did not complete." The previous version did not list this distinction, so the discussion conflated an empty result with a save failure. We are retaining two candidate return conventions for now: an empty collection means the query completed but found no relationship; null is used only when the relationship object itself does not exist. Whether to adopt this still depends on a readback from the most recent real call.

`lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb` can still serve as an inspection point for authentication-failure adjacency in the earlier investigation, but this review did not treat it as the place to implement rotation. What needs to be compared is the result actually obtained by the caller, not whether the filename can match both key and app at once.

The trial should first cover the old key, the post-rotation key, reading again after the save, and the read result when the watcher is missing. If any step requires the caller to save a temporary key, or if the watcher query changes the state after rotation, withdraw this combined trial and propose separate interfaces.

# API Key Rotation Review Plan

This proposal originally put two topics side by side because both started with application objects. Later review showed that what actually needs to be discussed together is the caller boundary, not turning rotation and watcher queries into one chain. The previous version had already split the two tracks; this revision fills in what each should promise and where callers still cannot be expected to infer the answer.

Rotation is a state change. The caller's required sequence is simple: obtain the old key, initiate rotation, receive the result, then confirm the new value from persistent state. If generating the new value and saving it are split across two layers, retries raise two questions: whether the value generated the first time is still valid, and whether the caller should continue with the old value or a temporary value after a failure. The proposal therefore retains the approach of having the application side perform this change; the caller is not responsible for holding a candidate key that has not been persisted.

An early draft made an inaccurate assumption: as long as a non-empty key was returned, the caller could consider rotation complete. That judgment has been dropped. A non-empty value only shows that a value was generated somewhere; it does not show that the value was written back, nor that the same value will still be returned on a subsequent read. The rotation result needs to be directly usable to determine success, while the key itself is checked as part of the post-save state.

The behavior boundary currently being trialed is: App#regenerate_api_key! must return true, persist a new token different from the old value, and the new key must satisfy `\A[0-9a-f]{32}\z`.

This requirement constrains only the application's rotation action. It does not specify when the UI should display the new key, nor whether other authentication entry points should refresh themselves. For the caller, the old and new values should be compared before and after the operation, not inferred from a watcher query or an authentication-failure page. An earlier troubleshooting record traced from the issue name and call name to `lib/overrides/devise/failure_app.rb`; during review, the authentication-failure entries adjacent to that location can be checked, but this entry point must not be treated as a conclusion about ownership of the rotation implementation.

The watcher query remains a read operation. It does not participate in generating, saving, or successfully returning the key, and its query semantics should not change just because the application has just completed a rotation. One question still needs an answer from caller samples: when the application exists but has no watcher, does the consumer expect an iterable empty relation, or does it need to distinguish "no relation" from "relation not obtained"? At this stage, the proposal leans toward having a completed query return an empty relation and treating failure to obtain the relation as a separate failure branch; this preference has not yet become a final interface contract.

Each track should be validated with a small set of samples. Rotation samples must cover at least four things: the old key before the operation, the operation's return value, the value read back after saving, and whether the read-back value differs from the old value. Relationship-query samples should cover only whether callers confuse these three states: the application has an existing relationship, the application has no watcher, and the read has not completed. Do not use "empty query" as a substitute for checking persistence after rotation, and do not return an apparently normal empty relation as a side effect of a failed rotation.

There was discussion of having the caller generate the key first and then pass the candidate value to the application for saving. This option has not been removed entirely because some integration entry points may genuinely need a preview value; however, it is not suitable as the default path. Once a preview exists, it must be clear whether the preview value is usable, whether it becomes invalid after a save failure, and whether retries reuse the original value. The existing material does not answer these questions, so the default rotation does not depend on it.

Withdrawal conditions are also handled separately for the two tracks. If the rotation operation returns success but the key read back is unchanged, stop releasing the change and retain the old key. If an empty relationship result cannot be distinguished from a read failure, do not yet connect the query to callers that require an explicit prompt. If both occur at the same time, do not conceal the cause with a single combined rollback; record the rotation-save result and the relationship-read result separately.

The only missing piece is actual caller samples: who reads the watcher relationship, how the consumer currently handles an empty result, and whether any integration entry point must preview the new key. Until those answers are available, the proposal defines only the application's rotation state boundary and does not extend into other parts of the authentication flow.

# Comment Compatibility and Tracker Troubleshooting Tree

2023-03-20: the on-call notes from the stability window started with a specific symptom: comments on the problem did not proceed to the tracker. At the time, the first check was whether Problem could read the comment condition, followed by the state of IssueTracker. Both looked like gates near the start of the flow; the person taking notes did not explain them separately.

```text
Comment did not proceed
├─ Does Problem have a comment condition?
│  ├─ No: stop at the problem object
│  └─ Yes: check the state of IssueTracker
│     ├─ Unsuitable: stop at tracker state
│     └─ Suitable: continue to adapter output
└─ Tracker output already exists
   ├─ Icon is empty: record the raw value
   └─ Fields are incomplete: record field names and values
```

The practice at the time was not to attempt the comment flow if `comments_allowed?` could not be found. If the condition existed but the tracker state was unsuitable, further checks also stopped. This made it easy to narrow the scope quickly during on-call, but did not establish whether both were actual prerequisites for comments.

Record icons and field metadata separately. An empty icon does not directly explain why the comment did not proceed, nor do missing fields prove that the problem object prohibits comments. Keep the return values, field names and values for the next review.

The old notes point from the problem name and call name to `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. Use this path as an entry point for review; do not infer ownership of the comment policy from the path name alone.

Open question: whether Problem's comment condition and the state of IssueTracker should jointly control the comment flow.

# Comment Compatibility and Tracker Troubleshooting Tree

The review of 2023-11-13 still starts from the symptoms observed in the field: the comment action may never have been initiated, or it may have passed the Problem object and stopped at the tracker integration point. Some records only say that an icon or field was incompletely displayed. All three symptoms were written on the same on-call ticket, which later made it easy to borrow causality from one to another.

```text
Field report
├─ No comment result
│  ├─ Action not initiated: stay on the Problem branch
│  ├─ Action initiated: check the IssueTracker integration
│  └─ State reading unsuitable: stop at the integration check
├─ Icon issue
│  ├─ Value present: retain the value and where it appeared
│  └─ No value: stop at the icon branch
└─ Field metadata issue
   ├─ Collection present: record the display name and value separately
   └─ No collection: stop at the field branch
```

## The Two Gates in the Initial Draft

The March draft wrote Problem and IssueTracker as sequential prerequisites. When the object did not have `comments_allowed?`, the record stopped at Problem; when the object condition was present but the tracker state was unsuitable, the record stopped at IssueTracker. Only after both passed did it inspect the display content returned by the adapter.

This sequence had one operational advantage: the person on duty did not have to inspect the Problem object, tracker adapter, and decorator all at once. It narrowed the troubleshooting scope. The issue was that the records only proved where the investigator stopped, not that the business boundary of the comment flow was the conjunction of those two conditions.

The old tree remains because later handoffs still contain short phrases such as "comment did not continue, state unsuitable." Removing it outright would make it impossible to see how the early judgment was formed.

## Objects Separated During Review

The review placed the Problem object and the tracker state in separate locations. Problem is the object visible where the comment flow is initiated; IssueTracker is another layer of state read only after the action has entered the area adjacent to the adapter. Both may appear on the same path, but when recording them, one empty value cannot be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

The new recording order is therefore narrower: first state whether the comment action was initiated. If it was not, write only what is observable on the Problem-object side; if it was, record whether it reached the tracker and what state was seen at the integration point. This change did not establish a final compatibility rule; it only ruled out treating the two locations as one master switch.

One review margin note was very brief: "A populated state does not mean that the state can determine whether commenting proceeds." It did not specify a new implementation, but it requires future records not to turn a readable condition into a business promise.

## Icon and Field Branches

The icon check asks whether the content delivered by the adapter is ready for the caller to display. If the return is empty, record it as empty; if its form is unclear, retain the original form. Do not fill in the encoding format here, and do not describe a missing icon as a comment failure.

Handle field metadata separately. When a field collection is present, record the display name and value separately; when only the field collection is present, record the gap at the collection level. The absence of a display name for one field is not evidence that the tracker request was never sent. Nor should the icon value be used to explain the field source.

Early notes grouped both issues under "tracker data incomplete." The term remains in old handoffs, but the review no longer treats it as a branch name. An icon is a display object, while fields are structured data; appearing next to each other does not mean they share a stopping reason.

## Failed Tightening Attempt

After review, someone changed the old tree to a stricter order: first validate the comment conditions for Problem, then validate the IssueTracker state, and only then allow the icon and field checks. The branches looked clearer, but display issues still had to wait for the comment issue to reach a conclusion.

If the field report only says that the icon is empty, this order sends the investigator back to Problem; if it only says that field display is incomplete, it first asks whether IssueTracker is in the usable state named by the old tree. The display-data anomaly is then subsumed by the comment branch, leaving only "comment did not continue."

This attempt produced no new conclusion. It left one operational correction: start with the actual return or action boundary for the reported category. Comments, icons, and fields can appear near the same tracker path, but they cannot be forced into a shared order.

## Entry-Point Boundaries

The old troubleshooting records use the problem name and call name to direct the reader to `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. The review still allows this location to identify the objects and outputs near the adapter, especially when explaining what "already reached the tracker" meant in the old records.

But this entry point is not a synonym for the entire comment policy. When the comment action has not left Problem, inferring the stopping reason from the adapter path puts the location in the wrong place; when the action has entered the adapter and only the icon or field is missing, the display gap should not be rewritten as a comment rule.

The path can help locate adjacent objects, but it cannot by itself say where a comment flow actually ended. The current record uses it only as the starting point; the exact stopping point still has to be recorded according to the action observed in the field.

## Provisional Wording After Review

The review did not confirm that "state unsuitable" is the reason a comment cannot continue. It requires retaining at least two observation points: the Problem object where the comment is initiated, and the state and return at the tracker integration point. Put icon and field metadata on side branches to avoid using unconfirmed corroborating evidence for the comment stopping point.

On-call notes are therefore provisionally written in three lines: whether the action was initiated; if it was, whether it reached the tracker integration point; and, if there is a separate display issue, what the icon and fields are. The three lines may appear in one record, but each line must retain its own object and stopping point.

This is not a complete replacement for the early on-call rules. The old rules will still appear in handoff screenshots and search results, and "stop first" served to narrow the troubleshooting scope at the time. They are simply insufficient to answer the compatibility boundary of the comment flow.

The unanswered question is: of the two stopping conditions in the old flow, which are only on-call safeguards, and which are actual code requirements?

# Comment Compatibility and Tracker Troubleshooting Tree

When this page is reopened, the situation is usually already muddled: a comment on an issue has not progressed, a tracker icon next to it is empty, and the field metadata is also incomplete. Early on-call tickets labeled all three as "tracker issues". Later reviews did not retain this umbrella term, but instead first looked for where the action had stopped.

```text
Anomaly report
├─ Comment has not progressed
│  ├─ Still in Problem: record the comment action boundary
│  ├─ Has left Problem: record the IssueTracker integration status
│  └─ Path unconfirmed: do not use icons or fields as a substitute for judgment
├─ Icon anomaly
│  ├─ Result returned: preserve its original form
│  └─ No result returned: stop at the icon object
└─ Field metadata anomaly
   ├─ Collection present: check display names and values
   └─ No collection: stop at the field collection
```

## 2023-03-20, the First On-Call Ticket

The initial issue was narrow in scope: comments appeared not to have progressed to the tracker. The record started on the Problem side, checking whether the object exposed the comment condition; if it could be read, the next step was to check the status of IssueTracker. That record did not distinguish between "the investigator chose to stop" and "the system required a stop", and both were written as the same stop branch.

The action tree recorded at the time is shown below, and it is retained to describe the old situation, not to reinstate it as the current procedure.

```text
Old on-call tree
├─ Problem does not have comments_allowed? → Stop at Problem
├─ Problem has this condition but the status of IssueTracker is unsuitable → Stop at IssueTracker
└─ Both look acceptable → Continue checking the adapter output
```

This wording was motivated by time pressure during the stabilization window. The on-call staff wanted to first confirm whether there were any obvious conditions on the object side, then decide whether to continue digging into the tracker integration. It did narrow the scope of the checks at the time, but it left no evidence of whether the comment action had been initiated or which layer it had reached.

The end of the same ticket also mentioned icons and fields. An empty icon meant recording a null value, and incomplete fields meant recording field names and values; default values could not be filled in for either when no content was returned. At that time they were still placed after the tracker output, which could easily lead readers to mistake them for contributing causes of comments stopping.

The entry point was listed as `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. Both the old issue name and the call name pointed here, so it became the starting point for reviews. The initial draft did not have enough material to establish this path as the sole home of the comment policy, and this point was retained in later versions.

## Early Margin Note: Narrow the Scope First

An unsigned on-call margin note read: "Do not keep guessing when the object conditions are unclear; stop for now when the status is unsuitable as well. " This sentence explains why the two locations were linked into one tree at the time. It was a protective operating habit, not a complete explanation of the relationship between the two layers.

Another margin note required the icon and field to be recorded separately. If the icon is empty, do not write it as "the field is empty"; if the field lacks a display name, do not write it as "icon encoding failed." Because how the calling side ultimately displays them was not recorded, retain only the form delivered by the adapter.

These two sets of margin notes were later placed on the same page, creating a subtle misleading impression: readers saw both "stop first" and "record display data separately," but did not know whether they had an ordering relationship. Later changes did not delete the original wording; they only added the actual branches beside it.

## 2023-06 Short-Lived Revision

At one point, someone tried to turn the flow into a stricter checking chain. First ask whether Problem has `comments_allowed?`, then ask for the IssueTracker status, and only then check the icon and field. The stated rationale was to reduce missed checks; in practice, however, this also deferred display anomalies until after the comment branch.

When a report contained only an empty icon, the investigator still went back to the problem object first; when a report contained only an incomplete field display, the investigator first confirmed the tracker status. Both kinds of report were forced through the preliminary comment check, so field notes continued to lump different phenomena together as "comment did not continue."

This change never became a formal rule. It left only the trace of a failed attempt: adding checks is not the same as separating objects. If the initial symptom concerns display data, start with the display data's return value; if the initial symptom concerns the comment action, first locate the action boundary.

## 2023-07 A Parallel Review

A review round received two pieces of information at once: the comment did not continue, and the tracker data was also incomplete. The first version of the record treated the latter as evidence for the former, but it was later discovered that the two pieces of information could not prove each other. The comment action may have stopped at initiation, while the icon or field may simply have been missing at the adapter output stage; their mere co-occurrence was not enough to identify the cause.

The review record therefore split the observed situation into three columns: whether the comment action started, whether the action entered IssueTracker, and what display data was actually returned. This did not fill in a new call chain, nor did it claim that the icon or field belonged to comment control. It only made it possible for the next record to identify the observation point.

That review also exposed a documentation problem. Writing only "did not continue" obscures the difference between an action that was never initiated and one that failed after it had already connected; writing only "tracker abnormal" obscures the separate gaps in the icon and field. Afterward, old records began to have wording such as "unconfirmed path" added beside them.

## Review Excerpt

At the review, the dispute was not whether the status had a value, but whether the status readout had the authority to determine the comment action. The discussion did not expand this issue into a new design, nor did it approve deleting the old on-call tree. The remaining requirement was very specific: observations on the problem-object side and observations on the tracker-integration side must be kept separate, and display metadata must not be used as corroborating evidence for a comment stop point.

The review also pointed out that `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` could be used to review adapter adjacency, but the filename alone could not be used to attribute all comment behavior for a problem to it. A path is an entry point, not a conclusion. If the action has not yet left Problem, inferring the cause from that file will put the record in the wrong place.

At the time, icons and fields were not compiled into a new master table. This was because the available evidence only supported retaining the original values and the gaps in the field set, display names, and values, not inferring the page's final appearance from those gaps or declaring on that basis that the comment workflow had failed.

## 2023-11-13, the old rule retained after review

The second version still retained the old rule of "continue only if both conditions pass," but noted at the start of the paragraph that it belonged to an early window. Retaining it served two practical purposes: phrases in the handoff records still needed explanation, and old troubleshooting screenshots still used this tree as their entry point. If the old rule were simply erased, the stopping points in historical records would appear to have no basis.

This rule is no longer treated as the complete workflow. It can only explain how the on-call staff at the time narrowed the scope. In particular, it cannot be used to explain the specific returns for icons and fields, because display data may appear separately outside the comment workflow.

The second version also relegated "incomplete tracker data" to a legacy term. It can still be used as a search term to understand old records, but no longer as a troubleshooting conclusion. The stopping points for an empty icon and an empty field set lie at different objects; missing field display names and missing values are also different types of gaps.

## Documenting the icon branch in the field

When a report involves an icon, first state whether the adapter returned anything. If it did, retain the return's original form and its location in the output; if it did not, record only that the icon branch is empty. Do not fill in the icon encoding format with a guessed value here, or infer from the icon's existence that commenting has already succeeded.

Icon issues and comment issues may lie close to the same tracker path, but they involve different observation steps. The comment branch checks whether the action has started and whether it has reached the integration; the icon branch checks whether the display object has supplied any content. Both branches can be recorded at the same time, but neither can substitute for the other.

Old records once described an empty icon value as "tracker data not ready." This wording is retained in the appendix because it is quoted verbatim from an old handoff; new records should specify whether the icon object returned nothing or the caller did not display it, and if there is no evidence for the latter, stop at the preceding level.

## Field metadata branch

The field branch first checks whether a field set exists. If the set does not exist, record the gap at the set level; if the set exists, record the display names and values separately. Do not describe a missing display name as the tracker request not having been sent, or use a default name to mask the original return.

Incomplete field display does not automatically change the status of the Problem either. It only indicates that some part of the structured display data lacks sufficient content. If the same report also mentions that the comment process stopped, the two stopping points still need to be listed side by side, and the field gap cannot be treated as proof of the comment rule.

This branch does not resolve how the caller ultimately displays fields. The old evidence only supports preserving the actual gaps in the field set, display names, and values. The scope of display remains an adjacent unresolved issue, and this page has not turned it into a new condition for commenting.

## Restrictions on using the entry point

When tracing back from `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`, first check which type of action the evidence from the case describes. If commenting has not yet been initiated, the entry point can only help identify downstream adapter connections, and cannot be used to fill in the reason for stopping on the problem-object side. Only if the action has entered IssueTracker is it appropriate to check the object relationships in the adapter output here.

If icon or field return values appear near the path, still record them under their respective branches. A file path does not replace an observation of a specific workflow, nor does it automatically become the root cause of all comment anomalies just because an old troubleshooting record points here from the issue name.

This is also why the old page retained both entry points and limitations. Entry points address "where to start reviewing", while limitations address "what not to read too much into once you get here". Both serve purposes local to this page, rather than constituting a complete set of tracker integration instructions.

## Two claims that were overturned

The first overturned claim was: the absence of `comments_allowed?` is enough to show that the comment workflow must stop. This judgment directly elevated the condition of being unable to read an object into a workflow rule. It can describe how the early on-call personnel stopped, but it can no longer describe the current compatibility boundary.

The second overturned claim was: when the IssueTracker status is unsuitable, the comment workflow necessarily cannot continue. This judgment turned a status reading from an integration check into the master switch for commenting on objects. Later records retained the status, but no longer let it override the actual point the comment action had reached.

There was also a related old claim that treated missing icons or fields as support for the judgments above. It was crossed out as well. Gaps in display data should remain in the display branch, unless an independent observation proves that they share the same stopping point as the comment action; this page contains no such additional material.

## Handoff addendum for 2024-02

During the handoff, someone reworded "comments did not continue" as "did not enter the tracker". This is closer to the action than the old wording, but it may still conflate two cases: the action was never initiated, or the action was initiated and then stopped at the integration boundary. The addendum requires that these two cases not be merged.

The same addendum also specifies that icon and field anomalies must not wait for the comment branch to be wrapped up. For icons, record the return value directly, and for fields, record the collection and gaps directly; if the two merely occurred at the same time on site, list them side by side in the same record, without creating a shared cause through the wording.

This addendum provides no new commands or additional entry points. It only fixes the recording granularity at the actions, objects, and return values that can already be observed. Do not fill in the next level if it has not been observed.

## Current troubleshooting tree

After several revisions through the early tree, the failed tightening proposal, and subsequent reviews, incoming reports are now routed by symptom. First ask whether the report actually concerns the comment workflow on a Problem; if not, do not use this page's comment branch.

```text
Current on-site triage
├─ Part of the Problem comment workflow
│  ├─ Action has not started
│  │  └─ Record the comment-related information seen on the Problem side
│  ├─ Action has started but has not left Problem
│  │  └─ Stop at the issue object side, do not invoke icon or field explanations
│  └─ Action has entered IssueTracker
│     ├─ Record the integration status and adapter return values
│     └─ Even if the status is abnormal, go no further than the integration check
├─ Only icon anomalies reported
│  ├─ Value present: preserve its original form
│  └─ No value: record the icon gap
└─ Only field anomalies reported
   ├─ Collection present: separate display names from values
   └─ No collection: record the collection gap
```

The current compatibility requirement is: Problem no longer publicly exposes comments_allowed?, and the status of IssueTracker must not block the issue-comment workflow.

This requirement addresses only the boundary of the comment workflow. It does not promise that the icon necessarily has a value, nor that every field can be displayed. The icon is still checked against the shape returned by the adapter, and fields are still checked for actual gaps in the collection, display name, and value; the two types of display issue must not be folded back into the comment decision.

## What the on-call record should contain

The comment report must at least state whether the action was not initiated, stopped at Problem, or had already entered IssueTracker. Writing only "comment failed" cannot distinguish these points. If the integration status is visible, put it in the integration branch, so that the status readout does not replace the action boundary.

The icon report must at least state whether a return value exists and whether the record stops at the icon object or at caller-side display. If no caller-side evidence is available, stop at the observed return shape. The field report must at least state whether the collection exists; when it does, identify which of the display name and value is missing.

When all three phenomena appear at once, they may be placed in the same incident record, but each must retain its own object and stopping point. Do not write them up as one overall failure just because they are all close to the tracker adapter. Only when a shared path and shared stopping point are observed again is it worth opening a separate review record.

## Remaining adjacent issues not yet split off

The comment compatibility boundary has been separated out from the old two gates, but the display scope for icon and field metadata has still not been finalized on this page. Between the field collection supplied by the adapter and the final display on the caller side, the current material does not further answer which gaps still belong to metadata and which already belong to the display layer.

Therefore, when the field collection exists but there is no readable display name, stop first at field metadata; when the icon has content but is not displayed on the caller side, stop first at the icon handoff. Neither case should reopen the early `comments_allowed?` branch.

This adjacent issue also explains why this page does not tabulate all icon formats, field default values, or client behavior. Doing so would turn unobserved content into rules, obscuring the action boundary currently established.

Another unresolved point is the object relationships near the entry point. `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` is sufficient as a place to revisit old records, but this path alone cannot answer the complete call relationships at every layer of the comment workflow. If object relationships need to be added later, they should start from the return and stopping points left by an actual workflow.

## Pre-release corrections for 2025-04-16

The most recent cleanup did not delete the old on-call tree, nor rewrite it as a clean current guide. The correction consisted of only three actions: mark the old tree as outdated, place the comment branch alongside the icon and field branches, and clarify the current compatibility requirement in its later position.

This correction also retained the question left by the review: whether the status value can determine the comment workflow. The answer is no longer implied by old phrases such as "status is appropriate"; instead, it is recorded according to whether the action has entered integration. This lets readers see where the old judgment came from and at which layer it was corrected.

Pre-release checks did not extend to other trackers, and the content of the related cards was not moved onto this page either. If you need to continue tracking the "issue comment compatibility strategy", you can look back via TRC-203; the on-site entry point for Tracker Icons and Field Metadata is still at TRC-218. The two cards serve only as navigation and do not replace the branch text here.

## Old Appendix: Quick-Stop Procedure for the Stabilization Window

The section below comes from an early handoff and deliberately retains its original shorthand. It is useful for explaining why old records often contain only the line "data not ready", but is not suitable for copying directly into current troubleshooting.

```text
Old quick-stop procedure
1. Cannot find comments_allowed?, stop.
2. The status of IssueTracker looks unsuitable, stop.
3. The icon is empty or the fields are incomplete, write "tracker data not ready".
```

Steps 1, 2 treated both object conditions and integration status as gates for the comment workflow, and were later superseded by the current compatibility requirements. Step 3 grouped icons and fields under a single label and could not distinguish a missing collection, a missing display name and a missing value, so it is retained only as a historical reference.

An old example also remains beside the appendix: start from the tracker adapter entry point for every issue comment. Now this is done only when the action has already entered IssueTracker; when the comment has not yet been initiated, stay on the Problem side, while purely display-related issues remain on the icon or field side respectively.

The old appendix has not been deleted, because its three phrases still appear in handoff materials. Readers need to know which different phenomena these phrases covered at the time, so they do not mistake historical stopping points for current rules.

## Closing Operational Boundaries

When a comment report comes in, record the action boundary first, then the integration status. When an icon report comes in, preserve what was actually returned for the icon; when a field report comes in, preserve the collection and the gaps in display names and values. Do not fill in caller-side results that were not observed.

Issue comments, tracker status, icons and fields may still appear along the same adapter-adjacent path, but this page does not recombine them into a single switch.
