# Decision on Tracker Creation and Delegation

Old links still bring "Issue Tracker Creation Boundary" and "Tracker Template Delegation" to this page. The two requirements were included in the same memo not because they had been confirmed to be part of the same implementation, but because, as Cascade 4.2 was being finalized, both happened to be followed up through Issue Tracker Integration. Only on a later review did it become clear that the earliest wording made "you can start looking here" sound like "this is where the work is completed". That distinction needs to be preserved.

The scope of this page has always been narrow: it only addresses the creation boundary, template delegation, and why the earlier investigation led to `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. It does not provide a complete description of tracker integration, nor does it summarize template formats, fields, or other adapters. DOC-17 records a separate set of interface review materials; the two pages being adjacent only means that both were brought back up during the stabilization window at the time, not that they share the same implementation assessment.

## Original Record: Two Different Ways of Asking

The decision recorded in the first version was not to combine the creation boundary and template delegation into a single "tracker workflow" item. That separation has not been reversed. The question for the creation boundary was: where responsibility ends as an issue moves from needing to be created to being handed over to the integration. The question for template delegation was: whether template selection or rendering is handed off elsewhere along with this action. Both statements include "tracker", but they trace different subjects.

The draft at the time also contained this sentence: "For now, treat the Unfuddle file as being near the creation entry point." This sentence should remain in the old version because it explains the direction of the early investigation. The old records contained only the issue name and the call name, both of which led people to `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. Without more local references, treating that module as the first stop was a reasonable way to organize the work; treating it as the final owner of the creation action went beyond what the records at the time could support.

The early text did not make this provisional status clear. It called for checking creation-related calls through the adapter before deciding whether to describe templates in the same place. There was nothing wrong with that sequence itself, but "near the entry point" was later read as "the entry point has been located". The old record is not being deleted because many regression notes still follow that path; but it can no longer support a judgment about implementation responsibility on its own.

## Approaches Rejected at Finalization

During finalization, combining the two subjects into a single item was discussed. The benefit was fewer pages, with readers needing to remember only "tracker creation". This approach was not adopted, not for the sake of tidy categories, but because problems encountered in practice arise in different places: some people cannot find the creation step when following the actual workflow; others can reach the creation action but do not know who should take over the template documentation. A combined heading would conflate these two ways of getting stuck.

Another approach was to list the Unfuddle adapter as the implementation owner for both tasks. This looked more explicit than the first approach and had appeared in early verbal retellings. It was not later recorded as a decision because the current materials provide only this Ruby module's local responsibilities and adjacent navigation links. The existence of the file, the ability to start the earlier investigation here, and the module name's connection to an issue tracker are all valid points; but directly inferring from them that template delegation is implemented here skips over the reference relationships that need to be rechecked.

The decision ultimately retained was narrower: keep separate records for the two subjects; use the Unfuddle file as a reference point for revisiting the earlier investigation; record the actual handoff locations for the creation action and template processing only after checking the corresponding references. This decision is not deferring the problem, but refusing to substitute one term for two subjects that still need to be checked. For finalization at the time, enabling regression testing to identify which part was missing mattered more than making an overly broad statement of ownership.

## The Retained Old Approach

> Old approach: infer from the adapter name that creation and templates are both on the same side, and keep only one entry point in the documentation.
>
> This approach was not formally adopted. It remains here because it explains why old links, earlier investigations, and the first draft repeatedly pointed to the same file. It is no longer suitable as guidance for new regression testing.

This old approach can easily give readers the wrong impression. The adapter path is indeed a concrete object, not an abstract label; but a path may serve only to lead readers to a local declaration or a neighboring call. The creation boundary might be confirmed near this module, or it might only become fully visible from the place that calls it. The same applies to template delegation. Being able to start investigating both subjects in the same place does not mean they end in the same place.

Nor was the "unified explanation" that followed the old approach carried forward. There is no longer a requirement here to put creation, templates, and all tracker-related terms into one paragraph. What needs to be filled in is a missing creation step in an actual user workflow, or the destination that gets lost when reading a description of template delegation; each type of addition should be attached to its corresponding subject.

## Diagram for Revisiting the Earlier Investigation

The diagram only marks the two verification paths branching from a single file location in the earlier investigation, not the execution order of the creation action or template processing.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Unfuddle recheck point" as unfuddle
  state "Creation boundary to be confirmed" as creation
  state "Template delegation to be confirmed" as template
  [*] --> unfuddle
  unfuddle --> creation
  unfuddle --> template
```

The diagram preserves the search method used at the time. It must not be read to mean that templates necessarily leave through this module, nor that the creation action necessarily ends in this module. The two paths are shown side by side because the old record brought both questions to the same recheck point; after that, the creation handoff and the template destination should be investigated separately.

## After the Cards Came Back

TRC-206 brought the creation boundary back to an actual user workflow. The card asks for the missing steps to be added back by walking through the workflow once, rather than further expanding the background. This changed how this page is used: when arriving at the Unfuddle file from an old link, looking only at the module name and historical notes is not enough; it is also necessary to see where in the workflow "needs to be created" becomes "handed over to the integration". Until this step has been filled in, the file location cannot be treated as the workflow boundary.

A review of the materials in September confirmed that the documentation had been revisited. The shared test environment was then temporarily unavailable, and the review produced no further material that could support broader conclusions. One earlier view was that the environment being unavailable affected only regression testing, not the ownership assessment. In hindsight, that statement understated the issue: ownership had never been established by the path in the first place, and the environment problem neither made it any clearer nor provided new evidence about template delegation.

TRC-212, by contrast, returned template delegation to hands-on regression testing. After the handoff was confirmed, the behavioral boundaries were rechecked in the quality materials through Issue Tracker Integration's existing entry point. This should be read as a reexamination of materials and an entry point, not as proof that "templates have already been handed over to Unfuddle for processing". The card asks readers who were not involved in the changes to follow the instructions and record the pages and links where they get stuck, which shows that template problems still need to surface through whether the instructions can be followed all the way through, rather than having the adapter name determine the conclusion.

Nor can the relationship between the two cards be interpreted in reverse. Adding missing workflow steps in TRC-206 cannot replace the delegation instructions in TRC-212; the hands-on read-through in TRC-212 cannot replace checking the references for the creation action either. They are kept together on this page only to help readers arriving from old records distinguish whether their next step should return to the workflow or to the template instructions.

## Where the Path Should Be Retained

`lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` should continue to appear in the recheck notes. It is a concrete location already used in the earlier investigation and is related to a local module for the issue tracker API. Deleting the path would leave the old records without an entry point and would also mislead later readers into thinking there had been no basis at the outset. Retaining the path does not increase its evidentiary weight.

When reading this file, it is reasonable to look first for creation-related calls, because that is exactly the clue left by the earlier investigation. If local references show an object being passed on from here, record that transfer location under the creation boundary; if references show templates being taken over elsewhere, record that destination under template delegation. Conversely, if all that is visible is a declaration, naming, or adjacent navigation, record only "rechecked here", not "responsibility lies here".

The old version placed "the actual relationships are still determined by the references" beside the path, which read like a generic caveat. This revision applies it to two specific questions: the creation boundary requires confirmation of the creation action's handoff; template delegation requires confirmation of where template processing goes. Without either of these two local relationships, the page can only preserve historical assessments and cannot add a new conclusion about the implementation.

## The Narrow Definition of Template Delegation

"Template delegation" on this page should not be expanded to cover all presentation, all fields, or all notification content. What remains is only a question of responsibility: whether template processing continues to be handled by the side where the creation action takes place, or is handed off elsewhere. Without supporting material, do not add template names, speculate about rendering order, or attribute every page problem a reader encounters to templates.

Therefore, the statement "templates naturally follow once creation is complete" is no longer used. It once made the records look coherent, but presented an unchecked connection as an established fact. If a later review confirms only the boundary of the creation action, this page should update only the creation section; if it confirms only the template destination, only the template section should be corrected. The two may ultimately connect, but they must be connected by an actual relationship, not by the wording of the documentation.

## Questions That Remain Distinct

- When continuing to trace inward from the old path, the exact point where the creation action is handed over to the tracker integration still needs to be confirmed by the reference relationships.
- Whether template processing is handled at the same location as that handoff, or is taken on afterward by another object, has not been settled by the materials on this page.
- Whether the workflow steps that TRC-206 asks to restore and the pages and links where readers get stuck in TRC-212 point to the same break cannot be determined from the two card titles alone.

These questions are not being retained in order to reverse the decision. What has already been settled is the recording method: do not merge the subjects, do not promote a historical recheck path into an assignment of responsibility, and make sure subsequent additions fall precisely under either the creation handoff or the template destination. The old page still has reference value because it preserves why the investigation initially started with the Unfuddle adapter; it is not suitable for directly assigning responsibility for the current implementation.

When someone next updates this page, they should retain the first draft's wording "near the creation entry point" and the explanation of its correction. Deleting it would make the old links seem groundless and erase a genuine change in judgment. New material only needs to answer one specific question: where the creation action is handed off, or where template processing goes. As long as the answer goes no further than a filename, module name, or name used in the earlier investigation, keep it in the recheck records rather than writing it into the decision itself.

Preserve the pre-upgrade Capistrano configuration and deployment artifacts, and record the differences between `env`, `default`, and the actual read location. Without call snippets, the differences cannot be attributed to Unicorn. For recovery, return to the pre-upgrade deployment combination; the specific recovery files were not preserved in the old records.

### Startup Order Changes Found

If later investigation confirms that Unicorn startup did not follow the old initialization order, first preserve the post-upgrade state, then restore the pre-upgrade order and combination. Do not directly delete the entry point at `config/initializers/devise.rb`, or change it into a new shared configuration location; this page contains no such migration decision. Checks after recovery should at least identify where the configuration was read and the connection between the deployment results and the regression.

### Only an Issue Name Is Visible, with No Calls

In this case, follow the old investigation path into `config/initializers/devise.rb`, but stop at file declarations or adjacency relationships. An issue name can help locate a candidate entry point, but cannot prove that a call occurred. Retain the regression description in the card and wait for actual calls and user outcomes; do not write "no calls" when the finding is "not found."

## Boundaries Between the Old and New Paths

"Old path" has two meanings on this page. One is the pre-upgrade Capistrano/Unicorn deployment combination; the other is the old investigation entry point that leads from issue names and call names back to the initialization file. Neither has a complete file list. The so-called "new path" also has only a provisional direction: continue using `config/initializers/devise.rb` as the starting point for verification while supplying the actual deployment calls. It is not an approved new deployment method.

The migration therefore cannot be executed as a fixed set of actions such as "copy the old configuration, replace the version, restart Unicorn." The input contains no actual records of these actions; writing them out directly would pass off standard practice as what happened in this incident. The only operations that can be retained are: preserve the old combination, check configuration sources, and confirm the relationship between startup and configuration reads; if a regression is found, stop before switching and restore the old combination.

## The Old Description of Responsibility Boundaries

The old page assumed that the initialization file was the place closest to the issue, and that compatibility between Capistrano and Unicorn could be assessed there in one pass. This is the obsolete part, retained for those who need to understand the historical assessment. This file can serve as an entry point for tracing back, but this page has no evidence assigning it responsibility for deployment, process management, or writing environment variables.

If further investigation continues, the person responsible for verification should separately record: how the issue name points to the file, which declaration in the file connects to `application` or `config`, and how the deployment process passes values to Unicorn. Without the latter two of these three parts, the page can only record navigation, not assign deployment responsibility. No responsible parties are supplied here on behalf of other projects or other pages.

## Actionable Stopping Points at This Stage

- No actual calls found: stop at `config/initializers/devise.rb`, add TODO, and do not declare the migration complete.
- Only configuration differences: preserve the old configuration and post-upgrade state, and do not switch the next batch yet.
- Regression confirmed to come from the upgraded combination: restore the pre-upgrade Capistrano/Unicorn combination, then preserve the regression results.
- Only a card status change: treat it as work progress, not compatibility verification.

TRC-209 moving back from In Progress to To Do corresponds exactly to the last case. It neither closed out the old assessment nor produced a new contract. The current page therefore retains the old path, the old rollback description, and the unfinished addition of actual calls; if material becomes available later, append it directly after the relevant paragraph rather than reorganizing this page into a new deployment specification.

# Decision on the Webhook Issue Object

The initial draft retained `public/javascripts/notifier.js`, limiting it to an entry point for the earlier investigation. That judgment remains valid. Later, TRC-215 was linked to support records; the to-do on the card was still to find a caller that still uses "Webhook Problem Object" and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. The link itself did not provide request body samples, nor did it connect the file to External Notification Delivery.

A later note on the card requested that it remain open for now, because one point about External Notification Delivery was still unconfirmed. The card then moved to In Progress. These changes indicate that the issue has returned to integration investigation; they do not establish object fields, a sending location, or runtime results.

## What the Old Entry Point Can Establish

The only code identified so far is still this short snippet:

```js
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

`ex` is a local value obtained from `options.e`, and `guess` is a boolean flag derived from `options.guess`. The function name indicates traceback printing, so it is unsurprising that the earlier investigation reached this file through an exception-related issue.

Previously, someone casually interpreted "exception object" as "Webhook Problem Object". That interpretation is now retained as an unverified earlier judgment. It came from the proximity of the function name, variable names, and issue name, not from call-related evidence. If this proximity is recorded as establishing where the object belongs, then once the actual send boundary is found, it will be impossible to distinguish verified relationships from what was only speculation at the time.

What can be recorded from the file is: the earlier investigation passed through here; the file contains `printStackTrace(options)`; that function reads two local options. What cannot be recorded from the file is: the Webhook recipient, the request body shape, the object's source, delivery timing, or whether the current call still passes through this module.

## Choices During the Stability Window

At the time, the choice was not between "continue investigating" and "stop investigating", but between several different ways of recording the findings.

| Choice | Treatment of the old path | What is gained | What is given up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Make a definitive determination | Record `notifier.js` as the object's implementation location | Quickly establishes a single entry point | Would turn function-local inputs into a claim about interface ownership |
| Keep only the name | Remove the file and function clues | Avoids mistaking the file for a definition | Cannot explain why the earlier investigation turned to the exception module |
| Retain with a narrower scope | Keep the path and snippet, requiring the caller to be found first | Historical leads can still be revisited | Cannot immediately provide an object specification |

The decision was to adopt the third option. The file path may still be included, but references to it must carry the context of an "entry point for the earlier investigation". It is not a claim about the current implementation location, nor is it a source for the Webhook object's fields.

This decision does not rule out either of two future outcomes: new call-related evidence may show that the file participates in object construction, or it may show that the file only handles exception display or tracebacks. With either outcome, the old record does not need to be deleted; it only needs to be treated as part of the historical investigation, rather than used as evidence for the current call.

## Terminology Breakdown

"Webhook Problem Object" refers to at least a few distinct layers in the materials from the stability window. Combining these layers into a single statement produces conclusions that cannot be verified.

| Role of the name in the materials | What is known | What is still missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Investigation topic | In TRC-215, integration issues are organized under this name | Whether the name corresponds to a fixed request body structure |
| Historical navigation | The old record points to `public/javascripts/notifier.js` | Whether the file belongs to the current notification chain |
| Local function | `printStackTrace(options)` can be located | Whether the function constructs the issue object |
| Current caller | The card requires the search to continue | Actual location, version, entry point, and result |
| External Notification Delivery | One point remains unconfirmed | At which boundary the unconfirmed item occurs |

This breakdown is not a specification table. It only specifies where new evidence should go. If a call location is found, add that location; if a runtime result is obtained, add that result; once evidence from the send boundary is available, only then discuss the request body. Facts already established in one column must not be used to fill gaps in another.

## Investigation Sequence

The subsequent investigation will proceed in the following order:

1. Use the issue name in TRC-215 to find a caller that is still in use.
2. Confirm the actual version at that caller. The old record contains `v_prev` for `internal/TRACE`, which cannot automatically be carried over to the new location.
3. Write down the entry point that leads into the call, rather than inferring it from the function name.
4. Record a result from a current run, distinguishing between "the code location has been found" and "the object actually reached the boundary that needs investigation".
5. Finally, compare the caller with `notifier.js` to determine whether there is a direct relationship.

Step 5 comes last to prevent the old file from dominating the current investigation. Continuing to read adjacent code in the same file can at most deepen understanding of a limited part of the module, and cannot replace confirmation of the current integration.

If no caller is found in the first step, the investigation stops at the first step. Do not invent what seems to be the most likely call location based on the old path. If all that is found is another piece of exception-handling code, it can only serve as a new local lead and cannot count as having found a caller of the object.

If the caller is found but the version is unknown, simply record the location and the missing version information; do not fill in `v_prev` at that location. Even if both the version and entry point are known, if a current result is still missing, the object must not be recorded as having already passed through External Notification Delivery.

## Current Decision

Maintain the approach of "retain the old path, do not make a premature determination about implementation ownership, and prioritize the current caller".

TRC-215 remains an entry point for the investigation. The support-record link and card status changes indicate that the issue is still being worked on, and cannot replace call-related evidence. If a direct connection between the file and the current caller is discovered later, document the connection itself; if the two are confirmed to be unrelated, also retain the historical fact that the old path was part of the investigation.

DOC-22 discusses English Error Count Localization, and can serve as a way to navigate to related materials, but does not provide evidence about the Webhook object's origin or delivery.

versions.body:
# Webhook Problem Object Decision

During the stability window, "Webhook Problem Object" was a name sufficient to prompt a search, but insufficient to support an implementation conclusion. The earliest investigation trail led the problem name and call name to `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. This location was never deleted afterward because it did explain the reading path at the time; but it repeatedly prompted the same misreading: seeing an exception-related function and treating it as the source of the external notification object.

This page's decision does not attempt to write a complete interface for Webhook. It addresses a more specific tradeoff in the stability window: when faced with an identifiable old file, an unconfirmed object name, and a card that has re-entered processing, which relationships can remain and which must wait until the current caller appears before being written.

TRC-215 is the card's entry point on this page. When the card was created, the observation was "Webhook Problem Object integrated into the daily usage workflow." The local to-do requires finding the caller still using this object and verifying the actual version, entry point, and current result. A support record was later linked to the card, followed by an additional note requiring that it not be closed for now, because External Notification Delivery still has one unconfirmed item. The card entered the in-progress state, indicating that the investigation had been picked up again; it did not add an object sample or replace the call location.

## Earliest File Lead

The old investigation pointed to the file `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. The fragment that can currently be located directly from that file is small:

```js
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

There are two local facts here. `printStackTrace` receives `options`; the function reads `options.e` into `ex`, and converts `options.guess` to the boolean value `guess`. The function name and traceback output are adjacent, so entering this location from an exception issue is not surprising.

But this fragment has no request body construction, no sending action, no recipient, and no field description for "Webhook Problem Object". `ex` is the exception value used by the function; it does not become a property of the notification object merely because the names are similar; `guess` is a local switch and does not become a delivery condition merely because it appears in the file. Locating the file and locating the object are two different things.

The earliest work notes did contain a convenient interpretation: since the function handles exceptions, the problem object might simply be the exception description here. This interpretation was not deleted because it explains why the old investigation stopped at the browser-side js module; but it is no longer used as a basis for judgment. It skipped the most critical part of the relationship: how, whether, and where the local exception handling becomes external notification content.

> Previous assessment: The problem object might simply be the exception description used by `printStackTrace`.
>
> Current interpretation: This function only shows that the earlier investigation examined exception-related code; it is not sufficient to establish the source of the Webhook object.

This correction does not mean that the old entry point has no value. Quite the opposite: the entry point is still worth retaining because it is an investigation path that was actually followed. What is being retracted is the wording that elevates the path into implementation attribution.

## What Needed to Be Decided at the Time

During the stable window, there was a seemingly convenient approach: first organize the "problem object" into field descriptions, then select possible fields from the exception-related code and add them. This could quickly produce a page that looked like an interface definition, but if the fields were inferred only from `options.e`, `options.guess`, or the function name, guesses would be written down as long-term facts.

Another approach was to delete the old file entirely and retain only the problem name. This would prevent anyone from mistaking `notifier.js` for the definition location, but it would also leave later owners unaware of why old material discussing external notifications had turned to tracing back through print code. A historical entry point that is no longer valid and a historical entry point that should never have existed are different situations; deleting the path must not conflate them.

Therefore, the stable window actually compared three options:

| Option | Treatment of the old path | Benefit | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct attribution | Record `notifier.js` as the Webhook object implementation location | Can immediately provide a single entry point | Local variables may be mistaken for object fields, and the file location may be mistaken for the sending attribution |
| Retain only the name | Delete the file and function, and write only the problem name | Avoids misreading file ownership | The actual direction of the earlier investigation cannot be traced back |
| Retain and narrow | Retain the path, function, and local snippet; inspect the current callers first | Historical clues remain usable, and the conclusion does not overreach | Cannot immediately produce an object specification |

The third option was adopted.

This decision does not mean that `notifier.js` is necessarily unrelated to Webhook, nor does it mean that it is already unrelated. It only stipulates that, without call-site material, "the old record once led here" cannot be rewritten as "the object is implemented here." If it is later found that this file participates in constructing the current object, that connection should be added; if it is found that the file only serves exception display or tracing back, that result should also be documented, while retaining the context that the earlier investigation reached this file.

## Different Objects Under the Same Name

"Webhook Problem Object" served more than one role in the stable-window materials. If they are documented as a single object at the same layer, some unverifiable statements naturally emerge, such as "the object is generated in notifier," "the object enters an external notification," or "the object is the exception description." These statements may respectively refer to the problem name, code location, runtime boundary, or request body, but no material connects these layers into a single fact.

The current record uses the following breakdown:

| Where the name appears | Meaning on this page | Content that can already be recorded | Content that cannot yet be recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Card topic | Search name for the intake investigation | TRC-215 Continue processing around this object | Whether the name corresponds to a fixed JSON structure |
| Old investigation path | Code location reviewed at the time | `public/javascripts/notifier.js` | Whether it belongs to the current sending path |
| Local function | Declaration that can be located in the file | `printStackTrace(options)` reads `e` and `guess` | Whether it constructs or delivers the issue object |
| Current caller | Location where the object is still being used | The card requires continuing the search | Location, version, entry point, and result are not yet complete |
| External Notification Delivery | Scope newly highlighted in the supplemental note | One item remains unconfirmed; the card cannot be closed | Where the unconfirmed item occurred and what result it produced |
| Request body object | Content requiring confirmation against the boundary materials to be sent | This page has no field materials yet | Fields, shape, and source |

This is not a field mapping table. Its purpose is to prevent newly added material from being recorded in the wrong place. Once the call site is found, record it under "current caller"; once the version is confirmed, write the version only at that call site; only after obtaining a result should you record the version and entry point that the result pertains to. Do not use local variables from the old file to populate the request body, and do not write a card status transition as a single execution result.

Once these layers are separated, the old path is neither treated as invalid noise nor elevated to evidence about the object. It preserves historical navigation; locating the object requires the entry point that is still in use, and that entry point must explain the version, method of entry, and current result.

## Limitations after the card was processed again

After the support record was associated with TRC-215, the tone of the investigation changed once. The initial draft only left "caller to find"; after the association, External Notification Delivery was explicitly retained as an unconfirmed segment. We cannot go too far here: association does not equal having obtained a delivery sample, nor does it mean that the known failure definitely occurred at the sending end. It only suffices to show that this gap still affects the integration judgment; it is not an item that can be automatically archived according to the old notes.

The supplemental note saying "do not close yet" has the same boundary. It does not state that the object is definitely missing, that the format definitely changed, or that the old js file definitely did not participate. It only prevents us from writing the existing clues as "the external notification has been fully investigated." Rewriting the status rationale as a technical attribution would create another layer of certainty without a source.

The card then moves to In Progress, indicating that someone has started handling it. The processing status is not a result. The minimum required content on the card remains the same set: a caller that is still in use, the actual version it uses, the entry point into that call, and the current result. If even one of these cannot be found, it must not be written as "Object definition confirmed".

This constraint avoids two kinds of rework. The first is guessing the interface based on the old js file, then discarding and redoing the entire section after discovering the actual call site. The second is seeing that the support record has been linked and writing "the issue has recurred" as "the delivery has been reproduced". During the stable window, the latter is what most needs to be avoided, because external notifications can pass through multiple locations, while the current evidence only confirms that one location remains unconfirmed.

## Processing Sequence

The sequence in the initial draft remains valid, but the follow-up review spells out the stopping point for each step more clearly.

1. Use the issue name of TRC-215 to find the caller still in use.
2. Once found, first confirm the actual version. The `internal/TRACE`-bearing `v_prev` in the old-file reference belongs only to the old troubleshooting entry; that marker cannot naturally become the version of the new call site.
3. Record the entry point into the call. The entry point should describe where this location is actually reached from, rather than inferring a call chain backward from function names.
4. Record a current result. The result must correspond to the call site and version confirmed above before it can show whether the object actually reached the boundary requiring investigation.
5. Finally, compare this caller's relationship to `public/javascripts/notifier.js`.

Putting the old-file relationship last is not because nearby code is not worth reading. Continuing to read further within the same file can improve local understanding of this module; it cannot resolve the gap of "whether the current integration passes through here". If a great deal of effort is first spent inside the file, the page will gradually become a set of notes on tracing functions and reading code, instead masking the fact that the original issue is still the integration status of the external notification object.

The diagram below only shows the verification sequence adopted by this decision; it does not indicate that a complete call chain has already been found:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Legacy investigation entry point\npublic/javascripts/notifier.js" as old_path
  state "Callers still using it yet to be confirmed" as caller
  state "Actual version yet to be verified" as version
  state "Entry point yet to be verified" as entry
  state "Current result yet to be verified" as result
  [*] --> old_path
  old_path --> caller
  caller --> version
  version --> entry
  entry --> result
```

If no caller is found in the first step, the investigation stops at the first step. Do not invent a "most likely" caller based on the legacy path, or treat another piece of exception-handling code as an equivalent substitute. If only the legacy entry point and local function have been confirmed, the conclusion must stop at "legacy entry point and local function confirmed".

If a call site is found but the version is unknown, record the site and the gap in version information. Do not fill it in at the new site simply because the legacy entry point includes `v_prev`. When the version is unknown, the call site is still a valuable new fact, but it is not yet enough to support a judgment about current behavior.

If both the version and entry point are available, but there is not even one current result, the record should stop at "the location and method of entry have been identified". This means the investigation has advanced one step beyond the legacy path, not that the object has reached the external notification boundary. This distinction is especially important after support records resurface: the support linkage proves that the issue is worth investigating further, but does not provide the result itself.

Only when all four items are available is it appropriate to look back and assess where the legacy file is involved. At this point, two equally valuable outcomes are possible: the call evidence establishes a relationship between the legacy file and the object, or the call evidence shows that the legacy file only explains the historical investigation and is not involved in the current integration. Both outcomes are more reliable than inferring object ownership directly from function names.

## Rejected shortcuts

### Listing function parameters as object fields

Someone previously suggested first listing `e` and `guess` as core fields of the issue object, then filling in the rest later. This approach was not adopted. `options.e` and `options.guess` are local options read by the function, and the available material does not place them in the Webhook request body. If they are included in the field table, readers will have difficulty recognizing that they come from function parameters rather than the object being sent.

This way of writing also has a practical cost: subsequent investigation will tend to validate predetermined fields rather than first confirming the object's boundaries. During the stability window, the "define fields first, find the entry point later" sequence is not used.

### Using exception display as a substitute for investigating external notifications

The old path is in an existing js module, and the function name also points to backtrace printing, so some people argued that the card's topic should be downgraded to a frontend exception-display issue. That classification was not adopted either. The creation observation for TRC-215 is still about the integration flow, and the later addendum still points to External Notification Delivery. A single old file is not enough to change the investigation topic to something else.

Conversely, the presence of Webhook in the topic cannot be used to assert that the old module is necessarily the wrong entry point. The available material is insufficient to make this either-or determination. The current decision requires the two tracks to be recorded separately for now, until the actual call relationship connects them or clearly establishes that they are separate.

### Wait until all materials are complete before retaining the decision

Another view was to remove this page first and rewrite an explanation after the complete chain was found. We did not do that. The stability window itself needs to retain the choices already made: why the old path is being retained, why it was not directly elevated to implementation ownership, and why the card was not closed based on the existing clues. Deleting these judgments would cause the next investigation to fall into the same kind of misreading again.

Therefore, the page remains, but it is not a Webhook specification page. It records what the investigation is allowed to use as a basis for proceeding when materials are insufficient, and which shortcuts have already been abandoned.

## Two wording corrections

The first correction addresses the wording "The old path proves the interface." After review, it should read "The old path proves that the previous investigation reached this file." The first wording turns a location into implementation ownership; the latter retains only the navigation fact. The latter wording is authoritative for now.

The second correction addresses the wording "The support linkage indicates reproduction." The support record associated with the card can only show that the issue has re-entered the integration investigation; the addendum still retains one unconfirmed point concerning External Notification Delivery. The current record uses "unconfirmed"; it does not describe it as "reproduced" or "located."

Neither correction removes any clues. `notifier.js` is still on this page, and the support linkage is still on this page. What changed was the way the clue was expanded into a conclusion.

## Boundary with adjacent materials

DOC-22 discuss English Error Count Localization. The two pages can link to each other, but the localized text does not provide the source of the Webhook object and should not be used to infer the boundary for sending external notifications. These two topics are not merged here because they use different investigation targets.

This page also does not cover a complete code walkthrough of the exception-display module. The function snippets confirmed in the file are sufficient to explain the old investigation entry point; without new call-related material, continuing to list adjacent code will not advance the investigation into the object. If a systematic explanation of `notifier.js` is needed in the future, there should be separate material for that module, rather than expanding this decision into a code tour.

## Current decision and addendum process

The current decision remains unchanged: `public/javascripts/notifier.js` is the location reached by the old investigation into "Webhook Problem Object"; the locally verifiable declaration in the file is `printStackTrace(options)`, and it reads `options.e` and `options.guess`. This supports historical navigation and local understanding of the function, but does not support identifying this file as the implementation owner of the Webhook request body or issue object.

TRC-215 will continue to serve as the investigation entry point. There are still unconfirmed parts of External Notification Delivery; the investigation cannot be closed merely because the old path exists, the support record has been linked, or the card has moved to In Progress. Subsequent decisions should first identify the caller that is still in use, and then confirm the actual version, entry point, and current result at that caller.

The next follow-up note does not need to rewrite the entire page. When providing the caller, add its location and indicate whether the version has been verified; when providing the version, add only the corresponding location; when providing the entry point, state clearly where the call enters from; when providing the current result, indicate the call location and version to which it corresponds. Only when a direct relationship between the old file and the current caller is provided should you add an explanation connecting them.

The core tradeoff left by the initial draft remains valid: the historical entry point can be retained, but it cannot vouch for the current integration. This stopping point is not an empty conclusion. It limits the next object to find to the actual caller, and it also limits the place most likely to be miswritten to the connections not yet established among the old file, function-local variables, the support association, and external delivery.

# Error Count Localization Plan

Initially, `config/initializers/devise.rb` was treated only as the lookup entry, with a preference for moving the sentence into the English translation. Later review did not establish that the initialization file owns the copy, so this remains a direction to try, not a decision that has been completed. The trial changes only the English display layer; it does not change the email-sending flow, other keys in the authentication configuration, or the caller's arguments. If the actual output also includes a following object name or link, use the call result as the source of truth and do not turn the half-sentence in the example into new complete copy.

**Translation catalog.** First check whether the corresponding key already exists in `config/locales/en.yml`. If it does, adjust only the singular and plural values; if it does not, confirm the key name used by the caller before deciding whether to add it. The benefit is that the English text is centralized, and rollback requires reverting only the localized translation changes. The cost is that the framework's plural-branch selection must be confirmed; do not assume that `has` and `have` will switch automatically just because their key names look similar.

**Handle it in the initialization configuration.** Keep the existing concatenation location in `config/initializers/devise.rb` and fix only the branch. This may be closer to the current call path, but it keeps user-facing text tied to startup configuration and makes it harder to determine whether other callers reuse the same logic. Keep this option only if the translation catalog does not actually take over the entry point.

**Have the caller choose the full sentence.** This avoids the unknown behavior of the localization key, but duplicates the English text; adding another language or changing the prompt later would require finding multiple call sites. Do not choose this option unless review shows that neither of the two options above is the actual output location.

Do not start the check by guessing ownership from the filename. Follow the existing call chain to find where count is passed, then record 1, a value greater than 1, and zero separately. Treat zero only as a sample pending confirmation; do not pre-classify it as singular or plural. Watch for three types of failure: the interpolation appears verbatim on the page; the number changes but the verb remains fixed as `has` or `have`; or initialization loading fails and the page never reaches the count message. If the third type occurs, revert the initialization-side changes first; do not use a successful startup to paper over unverified copy.

The later TRC-216 records retain only `toolchain_pinned`, so the toolchain used for reproduction is fixed. This can reduce environment differences, but it provides no caller output and does not decide text ownership for this page. Trial records must still preserve the actual singular, plural, and zero outputs; a fixed toolchain is not evidence that the trial passed.

It has not yet been confirmed which English form zero should use, or whether other languages share the same set of count keys. If code uses the complete English sentence as a match condition, the migration cost for the translation-catalog approach will be higher than expected; retain the old output, list the affected callers, and then decide whether to switch in phases. Proceed based on the singular/plural samples only if the caller uses it solely as display text.

When rolling back, restore only the translation items added or modified in this trial. If the initialization branch was tested, restore that branch as well, without making incidental changes to adjacent configuration. Until the review is complete, this document remains a candidate proposal: the trial scope, samples, and stop conditions are settled; copy ownership, the zero form, and whether callers need to be migrated remain to be confirmed.

# Slack Attachment and Link Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally started from a rather unreliable pointer. The issue name and invocation name led the investigation to `app/assets/javascripts/jquery.alerts.js`, so the initial draft assumed that this was the shared entry point for attachments and links. At that time, the symptoms were not separated: whenever something looked wrong in Slack, the investigation returned to this path and continued searching. This assessment is still retained in the old records because it explains why the wrong place was checked several times afterward; it is no longer used as the current ownership assignment.

During review, do not change the inspection order merely because you opened a file first. Copy down the results you see, then follow the tree below:

```text
Slack message has appeared, but the display is not as expected
├─ Only structured attachment content is abnormal
│  ├─ Attachment is still present: save the full request body; first check whether the structured fields are at the same level
│  ├─ Attachment is missing: save the pre-send object; distinguish between no attachment during generation and the attachment being discarded after sending
│  └─ Only one item is missing: record the specific field name; do not summarize it as "the attachment is broken"
├─ Color or title looks abnormal
│  ├─ color is abnormal: save the actual value and the caller's requirement side by side
│  ├─ title is abnormal: retain the original title; do not fill it back in with the text truncated on the page
│  └─ Both are abnormal: still record them separately first, then check whether they were produced by the same call path
└─ The message did not appear
   ├─ A pre-send object exists: continue through the sending caller
   └─ Not even a pre-send object exists: stop at the generation entry point; do not infer a relationship from this file path

The issue link is already present in the attachment
├─ The link cannot be opened
│  └─ Retain the complete URL; confirm whether it points to an issue page or an ordinary directory page
├─ The issue page can be opened, but it does not land at the canonical location
│  └─ Save the target address and line-number anchor in separate columns
└─ Both the target and location are correct
   └─ Record it as passing; do not recheck the link just because other attachment fields are abnormal
```

"Structured attachment" and "canonical issue link" are two adjacent but non-equivalent inspection objects. The attachment containing content does not mean that the link in it is canonical; the link being openable does not mean that the attachment fields were retained as specified by the original caller. Old records put these two things on one troubleshooting track, making it easy to stop prematurely after seeing a result at the first point. Now, if both symptoms appear at the same time, a raw result must be retained for each; only when the caller and the input are also the same should they be marked as the same reproduction run.

### Legacy wording from the path assessment

An old paragraph said: "`app/assets/javascripts/jquery.alerts.js` is the implementation location for the Slack attachment issue." Keep this sentence, but it represents only the working assumption at that time. Later review did not confirm from the current references that it handles attachment serialization or issue-link generation, so "reference verification pending" was added next to the field record. Do not treat the directory containing the file as a module boundary, and do not infer that it handles Slack just because the filename contains alerts.

If the inspection still needs to start from this path, keep the actions small:

1. First inspect the local declarations and direct adjacencies in the file related to `color` and `title`.
2. Then return to the caller that produces the Slack result and compare the pre-send object with the actual result.
3. If no direct reference is found, stop here and record "path checked, relationship unconfirmed"; do not treat similar names found through search as call edges.

The order of these three steps was added after review. The initial draft had only the first step, so it could explain why matching terms appeared in the file, but not where the result came from. The past practice of treating a "matched path" as a "found entry point" has proven insufficient; it is retained here to explain the source of the old assessment.

### Field notes for the link branch

When a link is problematic, the easiest things to confuse are the address itself and the location marker at the end of the address. First copy the complete link that was sent; if the copied content contains only an ordinary issue-page address, do not add an anchor based on the position shown on the page. If the address contains a locator after the filename, record the filename and line number separately. This record distinguishes the two failures better than "the link is non-canonical."

The old record did not leave a verifiable caller, nor did it provide the final result for any specific issue link. Therefore, no individual link can be declared fixed here. The original pending-investigation content of TRC-223 remains applicable: find the caller that still uses "Slack Canonical Issue Links" and verify its actual version, entry point, and result. After finding it, first write the caller version into the working copy, then return to assess whether this old path is relevant. Do not use the card name from TRC-223 in place of caller evidence.

### Retained judgment for the attachment branch

The attachment check handles only the visible structure in Slack output. If the attachment exists but its field content is wrong, save the difference between the pre-send object and the result; if the attachment did not appear at all, first confirm whether it was already present during generation. Do not use whether the link can be opened as a substitute for the attachment check, and do not use the attachment displaying normally to prove that the issue link landed at the canonical location.

TRC-219 works as navigation to the attachment entry point, but by itself it only leaves the requirement to "verify current-version behavior and identify an entry point for further checking." It does not provide an implementation relationship that can be directly copied back. Therefore, review records use the three-part form "result—caller—path": the result is the content actually seen in Slack, the caller is the confirmed location that produced that content, and the path is elevated to an entry point only once the reference relationship is established. If any one of the three is missing, stop at the corresponding branch.

### Remaining on-call notes

- When the same message has both attachment and link problems, save the results separately first; do not fix the color first and then treat the link as a knock-on result.
- Seeing only a match for `title` or `color` is not enough to show that `jquery.alerts.js` is responsible for generating the attachment.
- If the page opens but the location is wrong, continue along the link branch; do not rerun the attachment branch.
- Without the raw request body, you can record the symptom, but do not fill in the pre-send fields retrospectively.
- Without the caller version, retain the old-version assessment; it cannot be changed into a current-version conclusion.

These notes are more detailed than the initial draft, but they do not turn unconfirmed parts into fix conclusions. The current page remains a legacy troubleshooting entry point that can still be used for reference: it is suitable for triaging by symptom, but cannot replace verification of the actual call relationships.

# Decision on Traceback Links and Path Deduplication

This record was originally treated as a shared entry point for two work items during the stabilization window. It was retained not because the two work items had been confirmed to share an implementation, but because the earlier investigations both began around the term "traceback". As this entry point continued to be used, it became easy to connect the browser-side stack display, source links in reports, and path evaluation in the file tree into a hypothetical chain, so this record adds the approaches compared at the time and preserves the points where the earlier conclusions did not hold up.

The first path listed at the top of the record was `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. Only a very small snippet can be accessed directly at the frozen location:

```javascript
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

This snippet shows that `printStackTrace(options)` accepts an options object, extracts the exception object, and reads the guessing flag. It is enough to explain why the earlier investigation started with browser-side stack formatting; it does not show what kind of report the exception object comes from, whether the paths have already been deduplicated, or at which layer the source links are assembled. The old material turned "you can jump to this file" into "the problem is mainly in this file", and these two statements should now be understood separately.

The original plan was to read further through notifier first, then look for the causes of missing links and duplicate paths together. This plan had a practical advantage: everyone had the same short entry point for discussion, and the historical record would not be scattered across two topics. But it equated the starting point for reading with the location of the implementation. Continuing to make changes under that assumption could mean changing display code to address inconsistencies in path inclusion and exclusion; it could also mean standardizing file-tree evaluation to add missing source links. Neither action is supported by the available material.

Three ways of organizing the material were actually compared at the time.

The first was to keep both issues firmly tied to this js file. It was the easiest option, and the old records could immediately cross-reference the same location. The cost was inflating the limited information in `options.e` and `options.guess` into evidence for the entire traceback chain. This approach was not adopted; the file location remains as a historical navigation reference, but is no longer treated as the place to make changes for links or deduplication.

The second was to separate them completely by name and leave no shared record. This would avoid conceptual confusion, but it would erase some actual history: the two work items were indeed reviewed side by side during the same stabilization window, and both earlier investigations did go through notifier. Separating them completely would lead later readers of the old material to mistakenly believe that they had never been part of the same assessment. This approach was not adopted either.

The third was to retain this page and record the entry point they once shared and the rejected common-cause hypothesis; actionable verification would be documented separately. Source-link verification looks only at the original report, the source code, and the specific syntactic units that were changed. Path-deduplication verification looks only at inclusion and exclusion results within the same file tree. The shared section preserves only navigation and misinterpretations, and no longer represents a shared implementation, shared change locations, or shared verification results. This is the decision that stands.

The following sentence comes from an early assessment and no longer applies, but is retained here to make old references easier to check:

> Starting from the stack function in notifier should let us identify the causes of both missing links and duplicate paths.

The problem is not "starting with notifier" itself, but the way this frames the two phenomena under investigation as necessarily having a common cause. The locations identified so far do not establish such a common cause. It can serve as a hypothesis for reading the code, but can no longer be treated as a settled conclusion about the implementation. Another abandoned inclination was to unify the path rules first and then see whether the links could be restored; that ordering also skipped the inputs that each side needed to confirm separately.

The source-link work uses TRC-222 as its entry point for verification. This work requires running the source code for "Mongoid Backtrace Source Links" unchanged on the current version and circling the specific syntactic units that were changed. The focus here is the syntax and link locations in the report, not guessing the link format from variable names in notifier. The available material does not indicate which layer actually creates the links; therefore, "running it unchanged" is only a review step that remains to be completed and cannot be written up as if the links had already been restored.

The path-deduplication work uses TRC-226 as its entry point for verification. Its scope is limited to comparing inclusion and exclusion results within the same file tree, without changing the global user configuration. This restriction is kept fairly explicit: first obtain the actual inclusion and exclusion results from the local file tree, and do not use configuration changes to conceal differences in evaluation. If the local comparison shows inconsistencies, simply record which paths were included and which were excluded; do not recast this as a source-link compatibility issue, and do not invent shared rules just to make the two topics appear connected.

The two review tracks branch off from the old entry point, rather than deriving a dependency between them from that entry point. The relationship can be viewed as follows:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Old investigation entry point: notifier" as old_entry
  state "Source-link review" as link_check
  state "File-tree path comparison" as path_check
  [*] --> old_entry
  old_entry --> link_check
  old_entry --> path_check
  link_check --> [*]
  path_check --> [*]
```

The separation shown in the diagram only marks the boundary of this page's decision. It does not mean that the two topics can never intersect in the future, nor that notifier has no connection to either one; it only rejects using the current shared navigation as a substitute for a call relationship that has not yet been found. If subsequent review does show that both lead to the same section of the implementation, that fact should be added separately, rather than reversing the logic and making the old entry point bear the burden of proof.

Later records show that TRC-222 had entered an in-progress state, after which the behavioral boundaries were reviewed using the frozen entry point for "Error Lifecycle and Fingerprinting". This review did not merge the two topics back into a single issue, nor did it provide material proving that notifier is the final implementation location for source links or path deduplication. What it changed was how the old material is read: the shared entry point reverted to a navigational role, and each of the two work items retained its own object of investigation and scope of assessment.

The boundaries of responsibility are likewise kept to just two levels. The source code from the report, the link locations, and the changed syntactic units fall within the verification scope of TRC-222; inclusion and exclusion within the same file tree fall within the verification scope of TRC-226. This page preserves the rationale for the decision to separate these two scopes. For either side where the source has not been traced to a specific function, an implementation owner or change location should not be filled in here.

The remaining gaps have not disappeared as a result of this review: the locations identified so far do not answer which layer creates the source links in the Mongoid report; the actual call sites involved in path deduplication have not been confirmed on this page either; whether `notifier.js` has any other related display responsibilities beyond serving as a convenient entry point for the earlier investigation still needs to be documented separately in the corresponding work item. These gaps are the parts most easily overlooked as the old page continues to be referenced.

So this page retains the historical practice of "starting the review with notifier", but no longer treats it as a unified fix path. When the two topics appear side by side, first establish whether the task is to check report links or compare file-tree paths; similar names cannot substitute for call relationships.

# app cache and original state: trade-off decision

This discussion is not about rebuilding every old environment, but about deciding how to preserve the existing state as a first step. The two options are to keep using the fallback entry point or to separate problem aggregation from that entry point. Both options retain the cache; the difference is whether later reviews still treat them as the same kind of failure.

## Decision

Retain the current revision as the baseline for this check, without rebuilding the environment to restore the original state. Record problem aggregation separately and keep the fallback entry point, but stop using it as a shared explanation for both failure exits. This does not mean the cache is equivalent to the original environment; it just holds the objects already observed constant, so that new environmental differences do not get mixed into the assessment before the original command is recovered.

## Rationale

In `docs/adj-app/decisions/app-quality-signal-cache-vs-live-source-tradeoff.md`, the fallback entry point and problem aggregation correspond to different failure exits. If both segments remain under one entry point, samples that have gone through aggregation will be recorded as fallback issues. Even with new failure samples, we would then be unable to tell whether the change occurred before the entry point or at aggregation.

Two pieces are still missing from the available material: the original command arguments have not been recovered, and the current caller of the traceback line has not been confirmed. Neither provides sufficient grounds for rebuilding the environment. Behavior observed after a rebuild may come from the new environment rather than the revision at the time; continuing with the cache at least keeps the unresolved points in their original positions.

## Objections retained

The objection is that the cache can obscure the difference between reproducing in a single environment and rerunning in an environment on another machine; separating problem aggregation will also increase the number of records. That risk is real, so the fallback entry point has not been removed, and the aggregation record has not been made the new sole entry point. Both are kept side by side: the fallback entry point is for old values and rollback clues, while the aggregation record describes only its own failure exit.

For questions left by users, see DOC-32; this document does not decide the caller-side interpretation for them. Once the original command arguments are recovered, or the caller of the traceback line is confirmed, reassess whether the old entry point needs its priority restored. Until then, the current revision remains the cached state available for review.

Review trigger: compare entry-point priorities again only when both the original command arguments and the caller of the traceback line are available; if only one is recovered, keep this cached state.

This page is for one failed run for public-compatibility-catalog. Follow the sequence from that run; don't rerun it just to fill in the results. The most useful evidence from the run is the first thing that was missing; files or pages added later as stopgaps can't replace it.

Open the old entry point from `docs/adj-public/runbooks/public-compatibility-catalog-on-call-page-for-a-failed-run.md`, then find the place labeled "deployment link file." This name comes from the old record; the page doesn't specify its exact location in each deployment layout.

The minimal reproduction is the triggering event that already happened in the environment, not another attempt with a new set of conditions. First note the names and order of the objects you see; if both locations appear to show the same public-compatibility-catalog object, don't merge the records yet.

## When you see the first failure

1. Follow the old entry point through to the template rendering step.
2. If template rendering doesn't appear, stop here and mark this as the failure point. Don't clean up the environment or put manually rendered output back in the original location.
3. Keep only a record of the objects visible at the time, the entry steps, and "template rendering did not appear." Leave unknown preconditions unknown; don't infer success from the default configuration.

It means to stop changing the environment: don't replace the deployment link file, don't add the template, and don't collapse the two states into a single normal run. If template rendering has already appeared, this record doesn't apply; don't continue applying the return section below.

The old record required reviewing the deployment link file and the return action under different permissions, but it left no record of recovery results in the shared environment. If more work is needed, preserve the original objects and the sequence of the two states, then start cross-checking against the maintenance records for that entry point.

At the time, the failure was first attributed to missing template rendering. It answers whether the baseline point can be reached again after restoration; it cannot prove that all earlier summaries were identical. The fourth record is for objections raised by someone other than the author. Once the four records are separated, each answers only three questions: which revision was used at the time, whether the original command changed, and where the difference first appeared. If any question cannot be answered, leave that cell blank. The earlier practice of placing the first difference next to the migration notes would lead readers to treat relationships outside the directory as findings from the same check.

| Baseline | Original input and raw output | The directory has been adopted by a caller |
