# Cascade 4.2 Freeze Decision Record

This record preserves the choice made during the freeze window without smoothing over its nuances. The discussion was not about reorganizing all notification paths, but about confirming whether the persistence entry point should move along with Cascade 4.2, and what must be preserved first when an external hook fails. Beichen Operations Technology needed a decision that could be carried out within the bounds of the available materials; call relationships that had not yet been reproduced could not substitute for the decision itself.

## The Two Options on the Table During the Freeze

**Retain the current persistence entry point.**

This option kept the entry point that could be found at the time, limited the scope of changes, and allowed the existing path to remain the starting point for review. The initial trace led to `config/initializers/devise.rb`, but that was only a finding about location. The file location and call names led people here; that did not mean it had been proved that this file was responsible for the behavior as a whole. The materials also specifically placed `hook`, `rails`, `controller`, `model`, and `client` on the same tracing path, showing that reviewers were concerned with behavioral divergence after the entry point, rather than stopping at the initialization file.

**Adjust the window.**

This option aimed to move the persistence entry point into the new window, reducing how long the old path would remain in place. Its cost involved more than changing a location: if the full scope of the entry point's actual use had not yet been traced from the actual Rails entry point, adjusting the window would carry along observations and inferences that had not yet been separated. The freeze materials did not provide reproduction results sufficient to cover this change, so it was retained as an option that had been compared, rather than becoming an action for this round.

The choice at the time was to retain the current persistence entry point and defer the window adjustment. Here, "retain" was a compatibility decision for the freeze period, not a judgment about permanent ownership by a particular file. If someone later traced it to a different call boundary, that would not conflict with this decision; what would need to change was the window decision, rather than retroactively recasting the earlier location finding as an erroneous fact.

## What Was Actually Settled in the Meeting Materials

When an external hook fails, preserve the request body and status code first. This requirement is narrower than "check whether the notification succeeded" and more closely matches the actual situation. The request body preserves what the failing side actually sent, while the status code preserves the original result returned by the other endpoint. The two cannot be replaced with a single human-assigned explanation of the cause: the status code alone does not reveal the request content; saving only the request body also does not establish whether the failure occurred during sending, receiving, or rejection by the other endpoint.

The sequence adopted at the freeze was as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Actual Rails entry point] --> B[controller]
  B --> C[model]
  C --> D[decorator]
  D --> E[Notification client]
  E --> F[Preserve the request body and status code on failure]
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate only the tracing order required by the review; they do not prove that every layer necessarily calls the next. What can be seen directly in code or test output is recorded as observation; what is inferred from entry point names, locations, or call names is recorded as inference. Mixing these two categories was an error this review repeatedly sought to avoid.

## Earlier Assessments Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft treated `config/initializers/devise.rb` as a more stable home than the current version does. That wording was useful at the time because it provided a file that could be opened and did not invent relationships among people or modules; however, it did not cover the persistence entry point's path beyond the initialization file. Later follow-up tracing still produced no materials proving that "entry point location" and "permanent ownership" were the same thing, so the earlier assessment remained in the record with only its scope narrowed.

The initial draft also described adjusting the window as a course of action that could be completed along the way during the freeze period. That assessment was not supported by the actual review materials that followed. The review record was only sufficient to show that both approaches were still being compared; the window adjustment could not be described as already implemented, nor could "retain the current entry point" imply that all compatibility issues had disappeared. This reservation is not a new proposal; it only prevents the old wording from being read as a statement of completion.

The following matters were not collapsed into a single conclusion at the time:

| Recorded item | What could be said at the freeze | What could not simply be inferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config/initializers/devise.rb` | One of the tracing entry points | The permanent home of persistence |
| External hook failure | Preserve the request body and status code first | The specific cause of the failure is already known |
| controller, model, decorator, client | The prescribed tracing chain | Calls have been confirmed at every layer |
| Window adjustment | An option that had been compared | Already implemented in Cascade 4.2 |

The last column of the table marks the stopping point at the time. It does not present unknowns as rules; it preserves the boundaries of the evidence on which the decision was based. For hook failures in particular, only if the request body and original status code are retained can the next review distinguish between "the request was sent but rejected" and "the request was not formed at an earlier layer." These two cases were not merged at the freeze.

## Trade-offs After the Review

The direct benefit of retaining the current persistence entry point was avoiding simultaneous changes to the entry point and the compatibility window when the evidence was insufficient. The available materials supported tracing down from the actual Rails entry point and saving the request body and status code on failure; they did not support a conclusion that a cross-layer adjustment was already safe. The freeze decision therefore chose a narrower scope of action and left the window adjustment in the list of options not adopted.

This choice did not mean the old entry point came at no cost. Keeping the old entry point in place meant that subsequent reviews would still have to address the relationships among the file location, controller, model, decorator, and the notification client; looking only at `config/initializers/devise.rb` would again create the illusion that "the file has been found, so the problem has been pinpointed." The decision to retain the entry point accepted this cost in exchange for not expanding unverified changes during the freeze.

The sequence of "adjust the window first, then fill in the request records" was not adopted either. The request body and status code from an external hook failure are evidence from the incident; if the window were changed first, it would be harder to match the entry point where the failure occurred against the original records. The meeting materials therefore placed saving the request body and status code at the start of failure handling, rather than treating it as an after-the-fact cleanup task. Here, "first" refers to the handling sequence, not a judgment about the cause of failure.

## Review Addendum

The actual review added later did not provide enough detail to prove that the window adjustment had been adopted, nor did it establish `config/initializers/devise.rb` as the permanent home. The points that could still be retained were the same two: one, the actual Rails entry point is the starting point for tracing; two, when an external hook fails, preserve the request body and status code first. Other statements about cross-layer calls continue to be separated into observations and inferences.

This version therefore does not present the "review" as a success report. Without new code snippets, test output, or status code samples, it does not fabricate a completed outcome. It also does not delete the earlier preference entirely, because that explains why the current entry point was retained during the freeze rather than proceeding directly with the window adjustment. A decision record needs to retain both the chosen and unchosen options; otherwise, readers will see only a current statement detached from the review context.

For the switchover handoff of the notification integration on-call rotation, see DOC-44. Only the hook failure recording requirements connected to this freeze decision are retained here; the handoff content is not copied into this record.

## Objections Still on Record

The objection to adjusting the window was not that the window concept itself was unusable, but that the evidence at the time did not cover behavior after the entry point changed. Reproducing the issue from the actual Rails entry point first can put it back on the actual path; only by continuing through controller, model, decorator, and the notification client is there a chance to confirm the first divergence. If this path were connected by names alone, adjusting the window would disguise a working hypothesis as a compatibility conclusion.

The objection to treating the initialization file as the final home also remains on record. A file can be a starting point for the search, but it cannot by itself carry all the semantics of controller, model, decorator, and client. This objection and "retain the entry point during the freeze for now" can both hold: the former limits interpretation, while the latter limits changes. They are not two versions that contradict each other.

## Freeze Conclusion

For this round, retain the current persistence entry point; adjusting the window is not included in the freeze actions. When an external hook fails, preserve the request body and status code first. Start reproduction from the actual Rails entry point, continue through controller, model, decorator, and the notification client to find the first divergence, and record observations and inferences separately.

The scope of this conclusion ends here. It does not establish `config/initializers/devise.rb` as the permanent home, claim that the window adjustment is complete, or supply the next review with a failure cause that has not yet emerged. The earlier options, earlier location findings, and reservations remain on record for later assessments of why the scope of changes was not expanded during the freeze.

# Rechecking the Legacy Tracker in Notification Delivery

When taking over an issue around notification-delivery, the easiest mistake is to search directly for the adapter file based on the term "legacy tracker" and treat it as the entry point to the compatibility window. After review, that path can only serve as a starting point: the object provided by the delivery side and the object appearing on the adapter side have similar names, but that does not prove no conversion occurred between them, nor does it show that the compatibility check happened there.

This review follows a narrow path. Start at the repository entry notification-delivery and find one direct call site. At that call site, track only the object passed to the tracker. Do not fan out into the other delivery branches; follow this object to the first consumer that actually reads the compatibility state. Here, "consumer" means the location that reads the object state and uses it to decide whether the legacy interface is still available—not a wrapper layer that merely passes the object onward.

```text
notification-delivery
        |
        | Pass the tracker object associated with this delivery
        v
A direct call site
        |
        | Keep the destination of the same object
        v
The location where compatibility state is first read
        |
        v
The actual entry point to the legacy tracker compatibility window
```

The first call site is the most important anchor on this page. First check what it gives the tracker instead of guessing which adapter will eventually be called: if the object still carries runtime configuration there, the compatibility read later in the path can be compared against it; if the object has already been replaced with another representation, continuing to search by the delivery entry point's name will usually lead back to unrelated files. During review, inspect the object relationship before and after the call side by side. The goal is to confirm one transfer chain, not two local snippets that happen to have the same name.

`lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` is still worth opening, but it belongs after this narrow path. Because of the tracker adapter's naming, this file was previously treated as the first candidate. On rechecking, it is better used as a signpost for confirming the object shape on the legacy adapter side: when the object passed down from the call site reaches the adapter area, this file can help identify that the tracker-related branch is being used. But the presence of API or "tracker" in the filename is not a reason to skip the call site and declare this the entry point to the compatibility window.

The configuration-loading trace answers a different question in this review. The delivery chain tells us where the object comes from; the configuration-loading trace tells us where the compatibility state carried by the object is populated. The two should not be conflated into one call edge. The investigation sequence can stay short: first fix the object for this run at notification-delivery, then confirm that the direct call site does not replace it; next, trace how the configuration enters the runtime object; only then look downstream for the first place that reads that state.

There is an easy-to-misread fork here. Some files contain terms for tracker, configuration, and the legacy interface at the same time, so they look like a complete answer. But if they do not receive the object passed from the previous hop, they are only nearby signposts. Recording these files is still useful, especially when the entry point needs to be rechecked next time; the current path does not continue through them. This also avoids mistaking every tracker adapter for a consumer of notification-delivery.

The initial draft placed `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` too close to the endpoint; that has now been corrected. It helps locate the adapter context but does not determine where compatibility state is first read. The actual entry point is based on the first location where the object is read. If that location only forwards configuration or wraps the request, continue to the next read point; if the read result already determines whether the legacy tracker still takes the compatibility branch, stop there and mark it as the actual entry point.

This review does not need to list every notification channel. The current object comes from notification-delivery, so retain only this delivery entry point and one direct call edge. Even if other channels eventually connect to the same tracker, each must be rechecked from its own entry point; this path cannot be applied across them.

The remaining boundary is where the object conversion occurs. The review so far confirms that the investigation should start from the call site rather than the adapter file, and distinguishes configuration population from compatibility-state reads. But whether a unified conversion has already happened before the call site still needs to be supplied by the owner responsible for constructing that part of the object. Once the answer is available, insert the conversion point between the first and second lines of the diagram above; there is no need to rewrite the locating rules that follow.

# Deployment Sample Discrepancy Review

During the deployment sample review window, the visible result did not match the original plan. The minimum notice payload was still present, but the corresponding display could not be directly explained by the notes left before the window. The window therefore did not continue treating the sample as a confirmation result as originally planned; the impact was limited to the judgment made in this review and was not generalized into a conclusion that the deployment path had failed.

## What Happened During the Window

- Once the review began, the first finding was that the sample's visible result did not match the expectation set during preparation.
- The first comparison did not immediately show whether the discrepancy was in the sample content, configuration, or deployment process. The original plan only specified what should be seen and left no record sufficient to trace back the point of change.
- The minimum notice payload from that time was then retained as a fixed input for revisiting the issue. It can only prove that this input was still present during the window; it cannot show which stage rewrote the result.
- Temporary restoration used the original configuration file. The rollback drill was run using the original configuration file, which was the control point added this time; after the drill was completed, the review could continue, but the restoration time was not treated as the time when the root cause had been established.
- Before the review ended, the sample returned to an observable state. The window record did not provide a repeatable attribution.

## Impact Assessment at the Time

During the shift, confirmation based on this sample was paused, and a display that looked normal was no longer treated as evidence that the original plan had been met. The other preparation items were not rechecked individually on this page. This was mainly to avoid misrecording the temporary restoration as proof that the sample itself was correct, not because a larger release issue had been confirmed.

The input left in the record was minimal; when reviewed later, it still allowed us to distinguish between "the sample exists" and "the sample result meets the plan." The former was not lost during the window; the latter was not stably confirmed at the time.

## Earlier Assessment Retained

At the time, the discrepancy was tentatively attributed to an omission in sample preparation rather than to the deployment configuration itself. This assessment came from the surface result after restoration, not from ruling out the entire deployment process; the original record did not compare additional samples or break down the points of change one by one. This wording remains here to explain why the shift restored the review first, not as a conclusion for subsequent windows.

What remains unknown is whether the change that initially caused the visible result to diverge from the plan occurred in the sample, the configuration, or post-deployment processing; whether the minimum notice payload is sufficient to reproduce the same discrepancy in another window; and whether the rollback drill restored the display result or only restored the review entry point.

# Cascade 4.2 On-Duty Freeze Procedure

After receiving the freeze-time message:

1. Save notice-ingest's execution version, unprocessed results, and email-rendered samples.
2. Find the first raw failure; don't just forward the test summary.
3. At handoff, include the call entry point, shortest input, execution version, first raw failure, and confirmed responsible module.
4. Assign the first fork to the corresponding maintainer.

If expanding permissions, changing public behavior, or defining scope for the long-term owner is required, stop here.

# Notification Rotation Result Troubleshooting Tree

The ticket says the notification integration on-call rotation is complete, but the result has no verifiable point of reference. Don't branch first on whether the notification arrived; an email rendering appearing does not mean the rotation path was used.

```text
Inconsistent result
├─ Does presentation-mail's invocation entry point match the version shown on the ticket?
│  ├─ No: Stop at the entry point and version; add the invocation record.
│  └─ Yes: Use the same input.
└─ Compare the configuration loading traces
   ├─ Different: Run the rollback drill using the original configuration file.
   └─ Same: Record the difference and stop here.
```

When the entry point and version match, use only the same input; do not switch the email content or configuration file. When comparing the configuration loading traces, record the loading order each side went through side by side. If the traces differ at all, run the rollback drill using the original configuration file; do not switch to the new configuration during the drill. If the traces are the same but the results still differ, record only the difference and the entry point at that time, then stop here. The next step requires new invocation evidence or someone who can clarify the rotation's ownership; do not vote by repeatedly rerunning it.
